entities.summary: Abraham's son, the unique son of promise, who prefigures Christ in his sacrifice and marriage.

entities.title: Melchizedek
entities.summary: A priest of the Most High God who appears in Abraham's story, mentioned as another faithful individual who did not participate in the fallen worship of the nations.

entities.title: Ur-Nammu
entities.summary: King of Ur who founded the Ur III dynasty and initiated major building projects, including the Great Ziggurat of Ur.

entities.title: Hammurabi
entities.summary: A later Amorite king of Babylon, known for his law code, who lived about 500 years after Abraham.

entities.title: Søren Kierkegaard
entities.summary: Danish philosopher whose work 'Fear and Trembling' influenced modern readings of the sacrifice of Isaac, focusing on Abraham's perspective.

entities.title: Abram (Abraham)
entities.summary: The patriarch who meets Melchizedek after rescuing Lot. He refuses the spoils of Sodom and receives Melchizedek's blessing.

entities.title: Shemesh
entities.summary: The Canaanite sun god, of whom Zedek is a hypostasis. Worshiped in Jerusalem until Josiah's reforms.

entities.title: Zedek
entities.summary: A hypostasis of Shemesh, the sun god, associated with justice. The name Melchizedek means 'My King is Zedek'.

entities.title: Jerusalem (Salem)
entities.summary: The city of Melchizedek, originally named Urushalim, meaning 'city of Shalim'. Later becomes the site of the Temple.

entities.title: Belial
entities.summary: The demonic adversary in the Dead Sea Scrolls, who is judged by Melchizedek in 11Q13.

entities.title: Yam
entities.summary: The Canaanite god of the sea, often depicted as a dragon or sea monster. He is the embodiment of chaos and is defeated by Baal in Ugaritic mythology.

entities.title: Nero
entities.summary: Roman emperor (r. 54-68 AD) who persecuted Christians and is often identified as the antichrist figure in Revelation. The number 666 is associated with him through gematria.

entities.title: Lilith
entities.summary: A demonic figure in Jewish mythology, often considered Adam's first wife. In the episode, she is traced from Sumerian and Akkadian sources to the Bible and rabbinic tradition.

entities.title: Lamashtu
entities.summary: A Babylonian demoness associated with harming infants and pregnant women. She is assimilated with Lilith and later appears as Lamia in Greek mythology.

entities.title: Pazuzu
entities.summary: A Babylonian demon of famine and drought, invoked to ward off Lamashtu. He is known from the film 'The Exorcist.'

entities.title: Lamia
entities.summary: A Greek mythological figure, a serpent-woman who devours children. She is connected to Lilith and Lamashtu in the episode.

entities.title: Lycaon
entities.summary: A mythical king of Arcadia who sacrificed a child to Zeus and was transformed into a wolf, giving rise to werewolf legends.

entities.title: Wendigo
entities.summary: A spirit from Algonquian folklore, associated with cannibalism and greed. The hosts compare it to werewolf legends.

entities.title: Vrykolakas
entities.summary: A Greek term for a vampire-like creature, a demon-possessed corpse. The Nomocanon provides instructions for dealing with them.

entities.title: Joshua
entities.summary: Moses' successor who led Israel into the Promised Land.

entities.title: Gideon
entities.summary: A judge of Israel who encountered the Angel of the Lord.

entities.title: Hagar
entities.summary: Sarah's handmaid, the first person to encounter the Angel of the Lord in Scripture.

entities.title: Balaam
entities.summary: A non-Israelite prophet who encountered the Angel of the Lord with a drawn sword.

entities.title: Josephus
entities.summary: A first-century Jewish historian who mentions the giving of the Law by angels.

entities.title: St. Stephen
entities.summary: The first Christian martyr, who in Acts 7 mentions the Law delivered by angels.

entities.title: St. Justin Martyr
entities.summary: An early Christian apologist who identified the Angel of the Lord with Christ.

entities.title: St. Gregory the Theologian
entities.summary: A Church Father whose real self is his eternal identity in Christ, not his earthly struggles.

entities.title: Samuel
entities.summary: Old Testament prophet called as a child; the word of the Lord appeared to him bodily, standing by his bed.

entities.title: Jeremiah
entities.summary: Old Testament prophet; the word of the Lord came to him, spoke in first person as Yahweh, and touched his mouth.

entities.title: Ezekiel
entities.summary: A prophet in exile who is repeatedly addressed as 'son of man' (93 times in the book of Ezekiel), emphasizing his mortality and role as a prophet to the 'undead' in exile.

entities.title: Ancient of Days
entities.summary: A title for God the Father in Daniel 7, depicted as an elderly figure with white hair. This imagery is later applied to Christ in Revelation 1.

entities.title: Elisha ben Avuya (Aher)
entities.summary: A rabbinic figure in the Talmud who is portrayed as a heretic for believing in two powers in heaven. His story in Tractate Hagiga warns against this belief.

entities.title: Rabbi Akiva
entities.summary: A prominent early second-century rabbi who initially believed in two powers in heaven (interpreting the two thrones in Daniel 7 as one for God and one for David), but was later corrected in the Talmud.

entities.title: Prince of Persia
entities.summary: A fallen angelic ruler over Persia, opposed by the heavenly man and Michael.

entities.title: St. Christopher
entities.summary: Saint sometimes depicted with a dog's head, possibly connected to werewolf or giant traditions.

entities.title: Sasquatch
entities.summary: Cryptid possibly related to giant traditions or a hominid species.

entities.title: Sadducees
entities.summary: A priestly party in Second Temple Judaism that controlled the temple and corrupted the priesthood for financial gain.

entities.title: Watchers
entities.summary: Angelic beings who fell by teaching forbidden knowledge to humans and are imprisoned in the Abyss.

entities.title: Nephilim (Giants)
entities.summary: Offspring of Watchers and humans; their disembodied spirits become unclean demons.

entities.title: Gods of the Nations
entities.summary: Fallen angels placed over nations after Babel, who accepted worship and became demons.

entities.title: Prometheus
entities.summary: Titan who gave fire to humans and was punished by Zeus, paralleling the Watchers.

entities.title: Taj Mahal
entities.summary: A well-known example of a walled garden structure, used to illustrate the concept of paradise as a walled garden.

entities.title: El
entities.summary: The most high god in Canaanite religion, father of the gods, who dwells in a tent with his divine council.

entities.title: Baal Cycle
entities.summary: A Canaanite mythological text describing the gods' activities, including Baal's quest for his own place in El's tent.

entities.title: Julian the Apostate
entities.summary: Roman emperor who tried to revive paganism and criticized Christians for venerating relics.

entities.title: Eunapius of Sardis
entities.summary: A pagan Neoplatonist philosopher who mocked Christians for venerating the bones of criminals (martyrs).

entities.title: St. Nikolai Velimirovic
entities.summary: Orthodox saint who said a miracle is one of God's gifts at which men marvel.

entities.title: St. Gregory Palamas
entities.summary: Orthodox theologian who articulated the essence-energies distinction, used to explain God's work in the sacraments.

entities.title: St. Andrew of Caesarea
entities.summary: Sixth-century commentator on Revelation; stated that the devil fell after the creation of the world through pride.

entities.title: Simone Weil
entities.summary: 20th-century philosopher; contrasted ancient science as discovery of divine beauty with modern science as idolatry.

entities.title: Yam (Sea God)
entities.summary: Canaanite sea deity; in the Bible, 'yam' refers both to the sea and to this spiritual entity, which is subdued by Yahweh.

entities.title: Anzu
entities.summary: Mesopotamian giant bird; the Hebrew Ziz is its equivalent. Anzu stole the tablet of destinies from Enlil.

entities.title: Nimrod
entities.summary: Biblical figure described as a mighty hunter; linguistically identical to the Mesopotamian hero Ninurta who killed Anzu.

entities.title: Samson
entities.summary: Biblical judge; his death by pulling down the pillars of the Philistine temple is connected to burial under rocks as a cursed death.

entities.title: George Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
entities.summary: 19th-century German philosopher; the hosts say something nice about him for introducing organic development of concepts through history, used as an analogy for Scripture.

entities.title: Thomas Aquinas
entities.summary: Medieval theologian who used Aristotle's epistemology to argue theology is a science (episteme), not opinion.

entities.title: Donatists
entities.summary: 4th-century North African Christian sect that restricted salvation to their group; Fathers applied 1 John 2:2 to refute them.

entities.title: Marcian
entities.summary: Early heretic who rejected the Old Testament; the hosts note many Christians are functionally Marcianists.

entities.title: Father Andrew
entities.summary: The host of the podcast who reads the Gospel of Nicodemus.

entities.title: Hell (personified)
entities.summary: Personified as a character who argues with Satan and is forced to release the dead.

entities.title: Seth
entities.summary: Son of Adam who recounts the prophecy of Michael about the oil of mercy.

entities.title: Michael the Archangel
entities.summary: The angel who delivers Adam to Paradise and gives instructions to the witnesses.

entities.title: Enoch
entities.summary: One of the two witnesses who were taken to Paradise without dying.

entities.title: Penitent Thief
entities.summary: The robber crucified with Jesus who was promised Paradise and enters with the sign of the cross.

entities.title: Karinus and Leucius
entities.summary: The two sons of Simeon who were raised from the dead and wrote the account of the Harrowing of Hell.

entities.title: Joseph of Arimathea
entities.summary: The man who buried Jesus and later testifies to the resurrection of the dead.

entities.title: Annas and Caiaphas
entities.summary: High priests who question Joseph and later receive the writings of Karinus and Leucius.

entities.title: Nicodemus
entities.summary: A Pharisee who helps Joseph and receives the writings of Leucius.

entities.title: Pontius Pilate
entities.summary: The Roman governor who records the events in his public books.

entities.title: Deuteronomy
entities.summary: The book of Deuteronomy, particularly chapters 28-30, is the starting point for the discussion on blessings and curses, presenting them as consequences of covenant obedience or disobedience.

entities.title: Ugaritic Death Curses
entities.summary: The hosts reference ancient Ugaritic death curses as examples of cursing in the ancient world, involving invocation of spiritual powers and cooperation with demons.

entities.title: David Bentley Hart
entities.summary: David Bentley Hart is mentioned for his translation of 'makarios' as 'blissful,' which the hosts appreciate for capturing the divine connotation of the word.

entities.title: Nietzsche
entities.summary: Nietzsche's concept of eternal return is used as a springboard to discuss how eternal life begins now and is shaped by our present relationships and actions.

entities.title: Hades
entities.summary: The Greek term for the underworld, similar to Sheol, used in the New Testament and early Christian literature to refer to the abode of the dead.

entities.title: Sons of Korah
entities.summary: A Levitical clan descended from Korah, who rebelled against Moses and Aaron, but whose descendants survived and wrote several Psalms expressing hope for deliverance from death.

entities.title: Bart Ehrman
entities.summary: A New Testament scholar and friend of the show, whose views on the afterlife and the historical reliability of the Gospels are discussed and critiqued.

entities.title: Mari Documents
entities.summary: A collection of cuneiform tablets from the ancient city of Mari, containing prophetic messages from various deities, dating to the 18th century BC.

entities.title: Agabus
entities.summary: A New Testament prophet who predicted a famine and Paul's imprisonment, performing symbolic acts in the style of Old Testament prophets.

entities.title: King Saul
entities.summary: The first king of Israel, who experienced prophetic frenzy when encountering the Spirit of God, illustrating the disruptive nature of such encounters for the unrepentant.

entities.title: Enuma Elish
entities.summary: Babylonian creation account that was reenacted annually in ritual, serving as a myth that maintained cosmic order.

entities.title: Egyptian Book of the Dead
entities.summary: A manual for funerary rituals in ancient Egypt, containing narrative elements about Osiris and other gods that were enacted in burial rites.

entities.title: Torah
entities.summary: The first five books of the Bible, which functioned as a priestly manual and a guide for the community, with authority pointing to God rather than the text itself.

entities.title: Qumran Community
entities.summary: A Second Temple Jewish sect that produced the Dead Sea Scrolls, with a canon that included Enoch and Jubilees, and a focus on a solar calendar.

entities.title: Book of Jubilees
entities.summary: A Second Temple Jewish text that retells Genesis and Exodus, emphasizing a solar calendar and ritual laws, and was important at Qumran.

entities.title: Revelation of St. John
entities.summary: The last book of the New Testament, which had a complex reception history due to its association with chiliasm, but was eventually accepted as canonical.

entities.title: Shepherd of Hermas
entities.summary: An early Christian text that was widely read but not considered canonical, serving as an example of the middle category of authoritative but non-canonical writings.

entities.title: Molek
entities.summary: A demon associated with child sacrifice in the Old Testament, often mistranslated as 'ruler' or 'king.'

entities.title: Saint John the Evangelist
entities.summary: Author of the Fourth Gospel, traditionally seen as an elderly man writing a theological supplement to the Synoptics.

entities.title: Saint Kassiani
entities.summary: A Byzantine hymnographer and poet, known for the Hymn of Kassiani sung during Holy Week.

entities.title: Saint Augustine
entities.summary: Western theologian whose ideas on sin and guilt influenced later atonement theology.

entities.title: Peter Lombard
entities.summary: Medieval theologian who introduced the sufficiency/efficiency distinction in atonement theology.

entities.title: Father Vijay
entities.summary: A priest in the Indian Orthodox Church who asks about curses and the evil eye.

entities.title: Kenzie
entities.summary: A Bible college student from Colorado Springs who asks about the role of women in ministry.

entities.title: Travis
entities.summary: A listener who asks about sin, theosis, and demonosis.

entities.title: Kyle
entities.summary: A listener from Ireland who asks about the Second Coming.

entities.title: Phil
entities.summary: A listener from Canada who asks about legal language in salvation.

entities.title: Jonathan
entities.summary: A listener who asks about ancient Near Eastern cosmology.

entities.title: Genesis
entities.summary: The first book of the Bible, which contains the creation narrative and the story of the fall.

entities.title: Abel
entities.summary: Younger brother of Cain, whose righteous sacrifice was accepted by God, leading to his murder.

entities.title: St. Irenaeus
entities.summary: Church Father who saw the events of Genesis 4-9 (Cain and the flood) as the main event of the fall.

entities.title: Philo of Alexandria
entities.summary: First-century BC Jewish philosopher who wrote about Cain's curse and his alienation from creation.

entities.title: Eridu
entities.summary: Ancient Sumerian city, identified with the city founded by Cain in Genesis 4, traditionally considered the first city.

entities.title: Babylon
entities.summary: An ancient city in Mesopotamia, founded around 2300 BC, which became the capital of the first world empire under Hammurabi. In the Bible, it symbolizes human pride, idolatry, and opposition to God.

entities.title: Eber
entities.summary: An ancestor of Abraham, from whom the Hebrews derive their name. Mentioned in the genealogies, he is part of the lineage leading to Israel.

entities.title: Shamash
entities.summary: The sun god in Semitic mythology, worshipped in Babylon. He was considered the most high god, but was later overshadowed by Marduk.

entities.title: Thor
entities.summary: Norse god of thunder, son of Odin, known for his hammer Mjolnir and his battles against giants and the Midgard Serpent.

entities.title: Snorri Sturluson
entities.summary: 13th-century Icelandic Christian historian and poet, author of the Prose Edda, a major source for Norse mythology.

entities.title: St. Nicholas Cabasilas
entities.summary: Church Father quoted on miracles: 'Miracles are simply gifts from God at which men marvel.'

entities.title: Father George Florovsky
entities.summary: Theologian whose essay distinguishes dogma, doctrine, and theology.

entities.title: St. Herman of Alaska
entities.summary: Missionary saint cited as an example of evangelism through living among and serving a community.

entities.title: Jennifer Aniston
entities.summary: Actress mentioned in a humorous aside about being raised Greek Orthodox.

entities.title: Zachariah Sitchin
entities.summary: Author of ancient astronaut theories, mentioned in relation to UFO and ancient mythology connections.

entities.title: C.S. Lewis
entities.summary: Author referenced for the idea of the 'noble pagan' in the Last Battle.

entities.title: Timothy Patrias
entities.summary: Author of a book on the ethics of beauty, mentioned in the abortion discussion.

entities.title: Ray Comfort
entities.summary: Evangelist known for the 'Way of the Master' methodology, mentioned in the evangelism question.

entities.title: Enmerkar
entities.summary: King of Uruk in Sumerian legend, grandfather of Gilgamesh, who seeks to subjugate other cities through various means, including magical contests.

entities.title: Sagburu
entities.summary: A wise woman or witch who serves Enmerkar and defeats the sorcerer of Arata in a wizard duel.

entities.title: Sorcerer of Arata
entities.summary: A sorcerer sent by the king of Arata to curse the city of Eresh, ultimately defeated and killed by Sagburu.

entities.title: Nisaba
entities.summary: Sumerian goddess of grain, writing, and accounting, daughter of Enlil, associated with cows and the city of Eresh.

entities.title: Euphrates
entities.summary: A major river in Mesopotamia, called the 'river of the gods' in the epic, where the wizard duel takes place.

entities.title: Thomas Nagel
entities.summary: Philosopher known for the paper 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' which discusses the subjective character of consciousness.

entities.title: Elohim
entities.summary: Hebrew word for God or gods, used in the Old Testament to refer to spiritual beings including angels and sometimes deceased humans.

entities.title: Ruach
entities.summary: Hebrew word for spirit, literally meaning wind or breath, used in the Old Testament.

entities.title: Pneuma
entities.summary: Greek word for spirit, meaning breath, wind, or blow, used in the New Testament.

entities.title: Spiritus
entities.summary: Latin word for spirit, meaning breath or wind, from which the English word 'spirit' derives.

entities.title: Ghost
entities.summary: English word for spirit, originally meaning spirit in general, but later narrowed to refer to a particular kind of spirit.

entities.title: St. Basil
entities.summary: Church Father who wrote 'On the Holy Spirit' and affirmed the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

entities.title: Enkidu
entities.summary: The wild man in the Epic of Gilgamesh, who lived outside society and was seen as touched by the gods.

entities.title: Socrates
entities.summary: Greek philosopher who claimed a divine spirit (daimon) guided him, allowing him to stand outside Athenian society and critique it.

entities.title: Michel Foucault
entities.summary: French philosopher whose work 'Madness and Civilization' traced the changing concept of madness in Western history.

entities.title: Basil the Fool for Christ
entities.summary: A Russian holy fool who confronted Ivan the Terrible, embodying the prophetic role of divine madness.

entities.title: The Gadarene Demoniac
entities.summary: A man possessed by a legion of demons, healed by Jesus, and then sent to testify to his community.

entities.title: Saint Peter
entities.summary: Saint Peter is the apostle who wrote that baptism now saves us, connecting it to the flood of Noah and the descent of Christ into Hades. He emphasizes that baptism is not just a removal of dirt but an appeal to God for a good conscience.

entities.title: Jerusalem Temple
entities.summary: The Jerusalem Temple was the center of Jewish worship, but by the time of John the Baptist, it was seen as corrupt. John's baptism in the wilderness was an implicit critique of the temple establishment.

entities.title: Jordan River
entities.summary: The Jordan River is the site of John's baptism and Jesus's baptism. It is also where Joshua led the Israelites into the Promised Land, making it a place of new beginnings and reconquest.

entities.title: Pharisees
entities.summary: The Pharisees were a Jewish sect known for their strict observance of the Torah and separation from impurity. They generally rejected John's baptism because they believed they were already set apart.

entities.title: Noah
entities.summary: Noah is the patriarch who was saved through water in the ark, which St. Peter uses as a type of baptism. His story is connected to the spirits in prison to whom Christ preached.

entities.title: Maccabean Martyrs
entities.summary: Jewish martyrs who offered themselves as sacrifices for their people, foreshadowing Christ's voluntary self-offering. Their stories are told in 2 and 4 Maccabees.

entities.title: St. John
entities.summary: Author of the Gospel of John, which contains the Bread of Life discourse (John 6) and the account of the piercing of Christ's side, connecting the Eucharist to the creation of the Church.

entities.title: Passover
entities.summary: The Jewish feast commemorating the Exodus, which is a type of the Eucharist. The Eucharist is the new Passover, and Christ is the Passover lamb.

entities.title: Eucharist
entities.summary: The sacrament of the body and blood of Christ, which is a sacrifice, a meal, and a participation in Christ's self-offering. It is the central act of Christian worship.

entities.title: Roman Catholic Church
entities.summary: The Western Church that developed the doctrine of transubstantiation and practices such as perpetual adoration, which are contrasted with the Orthodox approach.

entities.title: Protestantism
entities.summary: A movement that arose in the 16th century, often rejecting the sacrificial understanding of the Eucharist. The hosts critique the reactionary positions that stem from this period.

entities.title: Tabernacle
entities.summary: The portable sanctuary built by Moses, anointed and filled with God's presence.

entities.title: Temple
entities.summary: The permanent temple in Jerusalem, first built by Solomon, later rebuilt, but never again filled with the glory cloud.

entities.title: Leviticus 8
entities.summary: The chapter describing the ordination of Aaron and his sons, including washing, vesting, anointing, and sacrifices.

entities.title: Numbers 17
entities.summary: The account of Aaron's rod budding as a sign of God's choice of the Levitical priesthood.

entities.title: Numbers 18
entities.summary: The chapter where God explains Aaron's duties, including bearing the sins of the people and guarding the sanctuary.

entities.title: Zacchaeus
entities.summary: A tax collector who repented and made restitution, demonstrating the connection between confession and restitution.

entities.title: Saint James
entities.summary: Author of the Epistle of James, which commands confession to one another and emphasizes the healing power of prayer.

entities.title: John Calvin
entities.summary: Reformer who considered church discipline a mark of the true church.

entities.title: Martin Luther
entities.summary: Reformer who had a sacrament of absolution and a version of public confession.

entities.title: Abraham and Sarah
entities.summary: The patriarch and matriarch of Israel, whose marriage is referenced in the Orthodox wedding service, and whose story highlights faithfulness to God and to each other.

entities.title: Isaac and Rebekah
entities.summary: Presented as the ideal married couple in Genesis, their marriage was arranged, yet Isaac loved Rebekah, showing that love is a concrete commitment.

entities.title: Jacob
entities.summary: The patriarch who married Leah and Rachel and had concubines, illustrating the problems of polygamy.

entities.title: Joseph and Asenath
entities.summary: Joseph's marriage to Asenath, a pagan priest's daughter, is expanded in the apocryphal text 'Joseph and Asenath', which portrays her conversion to Judaism.

entities.title: Malachi
entities.summary: The prophet who condemned faithlessness to the wife of youth and declared that God makes husband and wife one with a portion of the Spirit.

entities.title: Roman Wedding
entities.summary: The pagan Roman wedding ceremony involved sacrifices to household gods, a fake kidnapping, and a procession, which Christians could not participate in.

entities.title: Orthodox Wedding Service
entities.summary: The Orthodox wedding service references the patriarchal marriages, includes the reading of Ephesians 5, and emphasizes that God joins the couple together.

entities.title: Babylonian Gods
entities.summary: The pantheon of gods in Babylonian religion, including Marduk, Shamash, and others, who are seen as capricious and distant.

entities.title: Book of Job
entities.summary: A biblical book that addresses the problem of suffering, used as a comparison to the Babylonian Theodicy.

entities.title: Michael Heiser
entities.summary: An American biblical scholar and author, known for his work on the supernatural in the Bible. His passing is mentioned at the beginning of the episode.

entities.title: Apollinarianism
entities.summary: A heresy that denied Christ had a human soul, claiming the Logos replaced it. The hosts use this to illustrate the importance of understanding the soul correctly.

entities.title: Resheph
entities.summary: Ancient Near Eastern deity of plague, depicted as an archer. Mentioned in the Old Testament as a force under God's control.

entities.title: James
entities.summary: Author of the Epistle of James, which contains the command to anoint the sick with oil.

entities.title: Constantine the Great
entities.summary: Roman Emperor (r. 306-337) who converted to Christianity, legalized Christianity, and convened the First Council of Nicaea.

entities.title: King Charles III
entities.summary: Current King of the United Kingdom, whose coronation anointing oil was blessed by the Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem.

entities.title: Eusebius of Caesarea
entities.summary: Early church historian and bishop, a contemporary of Constantine, whose writings are a key source for Constantine's life.

entities.title: Lactantius
entities.summary: Early Christian author who wrote an account of Constantine's vision before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge.

entities.title: Julius Caesar
entities.summary: Roman general and dictator whose assassination marked the end of the Roman Republic and the rise of the Empire.

entities.title: Augustus (Octavian)
entities.summary: First Roman Emperor, who succeeded where Julius Caesar failed in establishing the Empire.

entities.title: Peter the Great
entities.summary: Russian Tsar who abolished the patriarchate and subjugated the church to the state, influencing later coronation practices.

entities.title: Ignatius of Smolensk
entities.summary: Russian traveler who witnessed and recorded the coronation of Byzantine Emperor Manuel II Palaiologos.

entities.title: Manuel II Palaiologos
entities.summary: Byzantine Emperor (r. 1391-1425) whose coronation was described by Ignatius of Smolensk.

entities.title: Pontius Pilate
entities.summary: Roman governor who condemned Jesus to crucifixion; Jesus told him that his authority came from above.

entities.title: St. Gregory of Nyssa
entities.summary: Church Father who preached against slavery, saying it was wrong to own another person created in the image of Christ.

entities.title: Theodosius I
entities.summary: Roman Emperor who made Christianity the official religion of the empire, about 70 years after Constantine.

entities.title: Roman Empire
entities.summary: The empire that Constantine ruled and Christianized, which became the model for Christian kingship.

entities.title: Byzantine Empire
entities.summary: The Eastern Roman Empire, which continued the Christian imperial tradition after the fall of the West.

entities.title: Council of Nicaea
entities.summary: First Ecumenical Council convened by Constantine in 325 AD, which addressed Arianism and established the Nicene Creed.

entities.title: Edict of Milan
entities.summary: Edict issued by Constantine and Licinius in 313 AD that legalized Christianity and restored confiscated property.

entities.title: Battle of Milvian Bridge
entities.summary: Battle in 312 AD where Constantine defeated Maxentius, after which he became sole emperor of the West.

entities.title: Chi-Rho
entities.summary: A Christian symbol formed by superimposing the first two letters of 'Christ' in Greek, which Constantine was told to put on his soldiers' shields.

entities.title: St. John the Baptist
entities.summary: The Forerunner of Christ, a Nazarite who kept his vows and is a model for monasticism.

entities.title: St. Anthony the Great
entities.summary: An early Egyptian monastic, considered a founder of Christian monasticism, known for his ascetic life and spiritual warfare.

entities.title: St. John Cassian
entities.summary: A monk and theologian who brought Eastern monasticism to the West, wrote the 'Conferences' and 'Institutes', and influenced St. Benedict.

entities.title: Tribe of Dan
entities.summary: One of the twelve tribes of Israel, often associated with idolatry and violence, and notably omitted from the list of tribes in Revelation.

entities.title: Mount Athos
entities.summary: A peninsula in Greece, a major center of Orthodox monasticism, associated with the Theotokos and the burial of a giant.

entities.title: St. Ephraim the Syrian
entities.summary: A fourth-century theologian and hymnographer who listed Samson among the dead in hell, indicating a negative view of him.

entities.title: St. Hippolytus
entities.summary: An early Church Father who called Samson a forerunner of the Antichrist, linking him to the tribe of Dan.

entities.title: St. Maximus the Confessor
entities.summary: Church Father associated with the doctrine of two wills in Christ.

entities.title: Mammon
entities.summary: A spirit of wealth and reputation that can become an organizing principle for one's life, leading to dehumanization.

entities.title: St. Constantine
entities.summary: Roman Emperor whose conversion established Christianity as a public religion, ending pagan sacrifices and making the Eucharist a public liturgy. His reign is seen as a key part of the restrainer.

entities.title: Joachim of Fiore
entities.summary: 12th-century Italian mystic who proposed a tripartite division of history into ages of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, predicting a future utopian age of the Spirit. His ideas influenced later millenarian movements.

entities.title: Montanus
entities.summary: Founder of Montanism, a 2nd-century heretical movement that claimed new prophecy and was chiliastic. His association with chiliasm contributed to its condemnation.

entities.title: Saint Cyril of Alexandria
entities.summary: A Church Father who interpreted 2 Corinthians 5:21 as referring to Christ as a sin offering.

entities.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
entities.summary: A civil rights leader quoted for the idea that the arc of history bends toward justice.

entities.title: William the Conqueror
entities.summary: The Norman king who commissioned the Domesday Book, which is related to the etymology of 'doomsday'.

entities.title: Reshef
entities.summary: Canaanite god of plague and war, identified as the first horseman (Pestilence) in Revelation 6:2, often depicted as an archer.

entities.title: Môt
entities.summary: Canaanite god of death, identified as the fourth horseman (Death) in Revelation 6:8, who rules the underworld and has a retinue of plague, famine, and war gods.

entities.title: Raav
entities.summary: Canaanite god of famine, identified as the third horseman (Famine) in Revelation 6:5-6, part of Môt's retinue.

entities.title: Thanatos
entities.summary: Greek god of peaceful death, contrasted with the violent death of the fourth horseman; not the figure in Revelation.

entities.title: Gog
entities.summary: Eschatological enemy in Ezekiel 38-39, possibly based on Gyges of Lydia, later seen as a type of the Antichrist.

entities.title: Magog
entities.summary: Land of Gog, possibly derived from Assyrian 'mat-Gugu', later identified with various northern peoples like the Scythians.

entities.title: Gyges
entities.summary: King of Lydia in the 7th century BC, possible historical basis for Gog, known from Plato's 'Republic' and the Ring of Gyges.

entities.title: Alexander the Great
entities.summary: Macedonian king who, in later legends, built a gate to imprison Gog and Magog, a story that developed in the Syriac Alexander Legend and Pseudo-Methodius.

entities.title: Hal Lindsey
entities.summary: Author of 'The Late Great Planet Earth', popularized the identification of Gog and Magog with the Soviet Union in dispensationalist prophecy.

entities.title: Bart Ehrman
entities.summary: A New Testament scholar and friend of the show, whose views on the Son of Man are discussed.

entities.title: St. Isaac the Syrian
entities.summary: Another Church Father sometimes cited by universalists, but the hosts argue his writings do not support the heresy.

entities.title: Origen
entities.summary: Early theologian whose views on apokatastasis were condemned at the Fifth Ecumenical Council.

entities.title: Theodore Abu Qurra
entities.summary: Medieval Arabic Orthodox bishop who wrote against Origenism and apokatastasis.

entities.title: Fifth Ecumenical Council
entities.summary: Council in 553 AD that condemned Origen and his teachings, including apokatastasis.

entities.title: Golden Calf
entities.summary: The idol made by Aaron while Moses was on Mount Sinai, representing an attempt to worship Yahweh through an idol, likely modeled on the Apis bull of Egypt.

entities.title: Baal-Peor
entities.summary: A localized form of Baal worshiped at Peor, associated with orgiastic fertility rites, which led Israel into idolatry and sexual immorality, resulting in a plague.

entities.title: Bronze Serpent
entities.summary: An object made by Moses at God's command for healing, later misused as an idol and destroyed by Hezekiah.

entities.title: Ark of the Covenant
entities.summary: A sacred chest in the tabernacle, with cherubim on its cover, representing the throne of God, not a container for God.

entities.title: Dura-Europos
entities.summary: An ancient city in Syria with well-preserved synagogue and house church, both containing extensive iconography.

entities.title: St. Phanourios
entities.summary: A saint known for helping people find lost items, associated with the offering of a cake called Fanouropita.

entities.title: Mesopotamia
entities.summary: Ancient region in the Near East, the setting for the historical texts discussed in the episode.

entities.title: Acadian Tablet
entities.summary: An ancient cuneiform tablet from Mesopotamia containing a text about a cleaner and clothing, used as an example of missing a party due to unclean clothes.

entities.title: Monkey Child
entities.summary: A humorous example from a cuneiform text about a slave woman who adopted a monkey child, illustrating a potential reason for being excluded from a party.

entities.title: Jester
entities.summary: A professional entertainer in ancient Mesopotamia whose stand-up routine is quoted in the episode.

entities.title: Proverbs 8
entities.summary: A key Old Testament passage personifying Wisdom, used to explain the divine Logos as the pattern of creation.

entities.title: Sisyphus
entities.summary: A king in Greek mythology who used techne to deceive the gods, including chaining Death. His punishment of rolling a boulder uphill forever symbolizes futile labor and the consequences of instrumentalizing the divine.

entities.title: Tubal-cain
entities.summary: A descendant of Cain in Genesis, described as the forger of instruments of bronze and iron. His invention of metallurgy is associated with violence and the misuse of technology.

entities.title: Apkallu
entities.summary: Seven sages in Babylonian mythology who brought wisdom and technology to humanity, often depicted as fish-men. They are associated with the origin of civilization and are imprisoned for their gift.

entities.title: Barbie
entities.summary: A cultural icon and toy doll, discussed as an example of technology that creates an artificial image of womanhood, reflecting the instrumentalization of human identity.

entities.title: Saint John Chrysostom
entities.summary: Major Church Father quoted on how people become like demons through sin, not through violent death.

entities.title: Aphrodite
entities.summary: Pagan goddess formerly associated with Thessaloniki, replaced by Saint Demetrius as the city's patron.

entities.title: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
entities.summary: 19th-century German philosopher whose view of history as the unfolding of the Holy Spirit influenced liberal theology.

entities.title: Arius
entities.summary: Heretic who refused correction from the Church, leading to his condemnation at the Council of Nicaea.

entities.title: Thomas Hobbes
entities.summary: Philosopher who proposed that all human actions are either self-centered or other-centered, with only altruistic actions being good. The hosts critique this as unrealistic and leading to absurdities.

entities.title: Sam Harris
entities.summary: Contemporary atheist author who proposes a utilitarian ethics based on maximizing well-being. The hosts critique his system for lacking a basis for altruism without God.

entities.title: Saint Maximus the Confessor
entities.summary: Church Father quoted on freedom: in the age to come, we will be free because we will be unable to sin.

entities.title: Henry Kissinger
entities.summary: Former U.S. Secretary of State, used as an example of a wicked person who prospered in this life, illustrating the need for a reckoning.

entities.title: Israel
entities.summary: The people of God in the Old Testament, whose history and experience Jesus embodies and recapitulates.

entities.title: God of Israel
entities.summary: The particular God revealed in the Hebrew Scriptures, characterized by humility and covenant faithfulness, embodied by Jesus.

entities.title: Jonah
entities.summary: Jonah's preaching to Nineveh gave the city 40 days to repent, illustrating the connection between the number 40 and the opportunity for repentance.

entities.title: Pentecost
entities.summary: Pentecost is the Jewish feast of weeks, celebrated 50 days after Passover, which commemorates the giving of the Torah at Sinai. In the New Testament, it is the day the Holy Spirit descended on the apostles, marking the renewal of the covenant.

entities.title: Great Lent
entities.summary: Great Lent is the 40-day period of fasting and repentance before Pascha, rooted in the biblical themes of preparation and purification, and originally connected to the catechumenate.

entities.title: Council of Jerusalem
entities.summary: The apostolic council described in Acts 15 that decided Gentile Christians were not required to be circumcised but were to abstain from idolatry, sexual immorality, and consuming blood.

entities.title: Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs
entities.summary: A collection of twelve apocryphal Jewish texts, each presenting the last words of one of the twelve sons of Jacob, written in the Second Temple period.

entities.title: Reuben
entities.summary: The firstborn son of Jacob, whose testament focuses on his sin with Bilhah and his repentance, serving as an example of overcoming lust.

entities.title: Levi
entities.summary: The third son of Jacob, whose testament presents him as the archetypal priest, with an apocalyptic vision and a focus on the priestly Messiah.

entities.title: Joseph
entities.summary: The eleventh son of Jacob, whose testament emphasizes chastity and forgiveness, and includes a dream vision of the Messiah as the Lamb of God.

entities.title: Mastema
entities.summary: A devil figure in the Book of Jubilees, depicted as a leader of evil spirits who makes a deal with God to afflict the wicked. He is associated with the giants and the angel of death.

entities.title: Angel of the Presence
entities.summary: A divine figure in Jubilees who speaks for God and is identified with the Second Person of the Trinity, often using 'we' when describing God's actions.

entities.title: Archangel Michael
entities.summary: Archangel who disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, as referenced in Jude 9.

entities.title: Ascension of Isaiah
entities.summary: A composite text with Jewish and Christian sections, containing an apocalyptic vision of Isaiah.

entities.title: Assumption of Moses
entities.summary: A testament attributed to Moses, likely written early first century AD, with a missing final section.

entities.title: Jude
entities.summary: Brother of the Lord, author of the Epistle of Jude, which references the dispute over Moses' body.

entities.title: Sammael
entities.summary: An archangel in Second Temple Jewish literature, often identified as the angel of death and the adversary. He is sometimes listed among the seven archangels.

entities.title: John Milton
entities.summary: English poet whose 'Paradise Lost' popularized the idea of a primordial rebellion of Lucifer, which is not found in earlier Christian tradition.

entities.title: St. Andrew of Caesarea
entities.summary: Early Christian commentator on the Book of Revelation, whose interpretation influenced the Eastern Orthodox acceptance of Revelation. He argued that the devil fell after the creation of the world.

entities.title: Simon Magus
entities.summary: A Samaritan magician who appears in Acts 8, offering money to the apostles for the power of the Holy Spirit. He was a cult leader with a Gnostic-like theology, claiming to be God and his consort Helen was the first thought of God.

entities.title: Sofronius of Tella
entities.summary: A 5th-century bishop who used the 'cheese sandwich oracle' and a divining cup to identify a thief, as reported at the Robber Council of 449. His story illustrates the persistence of magical practices among Christians.

entities.title: Witch of Endor
entities.summary: A medium consulted by King Saul to summon the prophet Samuel's spirit. The story is found in 1 Samuel 28 and is a biblical example of necromancy.

entities.title: Manasseh
entities.summary: King of Judah who practiced idolatry, sorcery, and necromancy before repenting. His story is in 2 Chronicles 33.

entities.title: Apollonius of Tyana
entities.summary: A contemporary of Jesus who was reputed to work miracles. Skeptics often cite him to challenge Christian uniqueness, but the hosts note that miracles alone do not prove divine origin.

entities.title: Carl Jung
entities.summary: Psychologist who studied Hermeticism, alchemy, and Gnostic texts, and collected the Jung Codex. He took these traditions in a psychological direction but also had a cult-like personal life.

entities.title: Kenneth Copeland
entities.summary: A prosperity gospel preacher whom the hosts explicitly label as not a Christian, accusing him of preaching magic rather than repentance.

entities.title: Benny Hinn
entities.summary: A faith healer and prosperity preacher, also labeled as not a Christian by the hosts, with a direct connection to new thought movements.

entities.title: Oprah Winfrey
entities.summary: Media personality associated with 'The Secret' and 'A Course in Miracles,' which the hosts critique as magical thinking with a veneer of Christianity.

entities.title: Urim and Thummim
entities.summary: Objects used by the high priest in ancient Israel to determine God's will, often seen as a form of divination but actually an accommodation to human weakness, distinct from pagan practices.

entities.title: Medusa
entities.summary: A figure from Greek mythology whose face was used on amulets and shields to ward off evil, based on the idea that the image of misfortune repels misfortune.

entities.title: Delphic Oracle
entities.summary: An oracle at Delphi where Apollo was believed to possess a person and speak through them, often giving ambiguous prophecies.

entities.title: Calvinism
entities.summary: A Protestant theological system that emphasizes predestination and God's sovereignty, which the hosts critique for presupposing God's subjection to time.

entities.title: Open Theism
entities.summary: A theological view that God does not know the future exhaustively, which the hosts argue makes God finite and not the true God.

entities.title: St. Mary of Egypt
entities.summary: A saint whose life story illustrates that identity is the whole arc of a life, including both sin and repentance.

entities.title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
entities.summary: Russian novelist whose 'The Brothers Karamazov' contains the 'Onion' folk tale used to illustrate the possibility of salvation through a single good deed.

entities.title: Karl Jaspers
entities.summary: A 20th-century German-Swiss philosopher who coined the term 'Axial Age' to describe the period of profound religious and philosophical transformation in the first millennium BC.

entities.title: Jericho
entities.summary: An ancient city in the Jordan Valley, continuously inhabited since around 10,000 BC. The archaeological site has been damaged by early excavations, making definitive conclusions difficult.

entities.title: Trudy the Tank Richter
entities.summary: Producer and phone screener for the show, known for her energetic presence.

entities.title: Melinda Johnson
entities.summary: CEO of Ancient Faith Ministries, present in the studio during the recording.

entities.title: Arianism
entities.summary: A heretical Christian movement that denied the full divinity of Christ, prevalent among the Goths.

entities.title: Gnosticism
entities.summary: A catch-all category for various sects that rejected the Old Testament and the goodness of creation, often mixing Christian elements with pagan philosophy.

entities.title: Neoplatonism
entities.summary: A philosophical system developed by Plotinus that borrowed Christian ideas to compete with Christianity, but remained fundamentally pagan.

entities.title: Leontopolis
entities.summary: Site of a Jewish temple in Egypt that operated alongside the Jerusalem Temple, showing diversity in Second Temple Judaism.

entities.title: Elephantine Island
entities.summary: An island in the Nile where a Jewish temple may have existed, further evidence of non-centralized worship.

entities.title: Karl Marx
entities.summary: Philosopher and economist, considered a peak modernist for his theory of historical development.

entities.title: Jacques Derrida
entities.summary: French philosopher, a key figure in post-structuralism, known for deconstruction.

entities.title: Friedrich Nietzsche
entities.summary: German philosopher, critiqued modernism and proposed perspectivism and the great man theory of history.

entities.title: Edmund Burke
entities.summary: Irish statesman and philosopher, founding father of traditional conservatism, critiqued the French Revolution.

entities.title: Terry Eagleton
entities.summary: Marxist literary theorist, author of 'The Illusions of Postmodernism'.

entities.title: Hesiod
entities.summary: Ancient Greek poet, author of the Theogony and Works and Days, which describe the origins of the gods and the daemons.

entities.title: Justin Martyr
entities.summary: Second-century Christian apologist who identified the Greek gods as demons, the offspring of fallen angels and women.

entities.title: Athenagoras
entities.summary: Second-century Christian apologist who wrote that demons are the souls of the giants, the offspring of fallen angels.

entities.title: John Chrysostom
entities.summary: Fourth-century Church Father who argued that demons are not the souls of the violently dead but of those who live in sin, imitating demons.

entities.title: Augustine
entities.summary: Fourth/fifth-century Church Father who rejected the literal view of angels mating with women, but his arguments contain pieces of the earlier view.

entities.title: Jacob and Esau
entities.summary: Jacob and Esau are twin brothers in Genesis. The hosts argue that Paul's reference to 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' is about nations, not individuals, and refers to the Edomites' betrayal of Israel, not their eternal destiny.

entities.title: Ignatius of Antioch
entities.summary: An early Church Father and disciple of the Apostle John, who wrote seven letters against Docetism, emphasizing the reality of Christ's flesh.

entities.title: Cerinthus
entities.summary: An early heretic who taught that Jesus was a man upon whom the divine Logos descended at his baptism, a form of adoptionism.

entities.title: Francis Fukuyama
entities.summary: Author of 'The End of History' who argued that liberal democracy represents the endpoint of human ideological evolution. The hosts use his book as an example of a secular teleology.

entities.title: Gregory of Nyssa
entities.summary: 4th-century Church Father known for his opposition to slavery. The hosts cite him as an example of how Christian transformation led to the abolition of slavery.

entities.title: Book of Leviticus
entities.summary: The primary source for laws of clean and unclean, including the distinction between holy and common, and the procedures for purification.

entities.title: King David
entities.summary: Example of repentance and acceptance of permanent ritual impurity, as he was not allowed to build the temple due to bloodshed, yet his sin was forgiven.

entities.title: Asmodius
entities.summary: A demon in the Book of Tobit, whose name means 'wrath demon' in Persian. He is associated with wrath, shrine prostitution, and has a long afterlife in Jewish and Islamic traditions, sometimes identified as the disembodied spirit of Hadad the Edomite.

entities.title: King Saul
entities.summary: First king of Israel, who after his disobedience was troubled by an unclean spirit sent by God. This torment was intended to drive him to repentance but instead led to rage and murderous intent toward David.

entities.title: Sarah of Tobit
entities.summary: A woman in the Book of Tobit who was afflicted by the demon Asmodius, which killed her previous seven husbands on their wedding nights. She is a victim of ancestral sin and is delivered by Tobias with the help of the Archangel Raphael.

entities.title: Hadad the Edomite
entities.summary: An Edomite royal who escaped to Egypt and later became an adversary of Solomon. In later Jewish tradition, he is identified as the illegitimate son of David through a shrine prostitute, and his disembodied spirit is said to be Asmodius.

entities.title: Dionysius the Areopagite
entities.summary: Early Christian theologian who wrote 'The Celestial Hierarchy', which systematized the nine ranks of angels and influenced Orthodox angelology.

entities.title: Archangel Gabriel
entities.summary: An archangel who appears in Scripture delivering messages, including the Annunciation to the Theotokos. He is one of the seven chief angels.

entities.title: St. Michael
entities.summary: Archangel mentioned in Scripture and tradition, often depicted as a warrior and leader of the heavenly host. In some traditions, he is considered a Seraphim.

entities.title: Yehoel
entities.summary: An angelic being in the Apocalypse of Abraham, bearing the name of God, acting as a priest and guide, representing a second power in heaven.

entities.title: Bogomils
entities.summary: Medieval dualist sect in the Balkans that preserved the Apocalypse of Abraham, holding Gnostic-like beliefs.

entities.title: St. Epiphanius of Salamis
entities.summary: Church Father who mentioned a Gnostic text called the Apocalypse of Abraham, likely different from the Slavonic text.

entities.title: Deuteronomy 21
entities.summary: Old Testament passage about capital punishment and the curse of hanging on a tree, foundational for understanding the New Testament view of Christ's crucifixion.

entities.title: Day of Atonement
entities.summary: The annual Old Testament ritual involving two goats, one sacrificed and one sent into the wilderness, foreshadowing Christ's atoning work.

entities.title: Edomites
entities.summary: Descendants of Esau, a non-Israelite Abrahamite group that initially worshiped Yahweh and received land from God.

entities.title: Moabites
entities.summary: Descendants of Lot, another non-Israelite Abrahamite group that received land and were treated similarly to Israel.

entities.title: Dispensationalism
entities.summary: A theological system that separates Israel and the Church, often linking the modern state of Israel to biblical prophecy. The hosts critique it heavily.

entities.title: Tribe of Dan
entities.summary: A tribe of Israel that may have originated from the Sea Peoples (Danai), not primarily biological descendants of Jacob. They were poorly assimilated and later fell into idolatry.

entities.title: Assyrians
entities.summary: The Assyrian Empire destroyed the Northern Kingdom of Israel in 722 BC. They were known for extreme brutality, including mass executions and deportations, and their capital was Nineveh.

entities.title: Amalekites
entities.summary: The Amalekites were a giant clan descended from Esau, uniquely belligerent toward Israel. They attacked Israel at Mount Sinai, and God commanded their destruction. Saul's failure to fully execute this command led to his rejection.

entities.title: Cyrus the Great
entities.summary: Founder of the Persian Achaemenid Empire, who allowed the Jewish exiles to return to Judea and rebuild the Temple. He is referred to as 'Messiah' in the Hebrew Scriptures.

entities.title: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
entities.summary: Seleucid king who persecuted the Jews, desecrated the Temple, and triggered the Maccabean Revolt. His actions are seen as the 'abomination of desolation'.

entities.title: Judas Maccabeus
entities.summary: Leader of the Maccabean Revolt, known as 'Judah the Hammer'. He recaptured and rededicated the Temple, an event commemorated by Hanukkah.

entities.title: John Hyrcanus
entities.summary: Hasmonean king and high priest who expanded Judea by conquering Samaria and Idumea, destroying the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim.

entities.title: Samaritans
entities.summary: A group with mixed ancestry from the northern kingdom and foreign settlers, who had their own version of the Torah and worshiped on Mount Gerizim. They were rivals of the Judeans.

entities.title: Seleucid Empire
entities.summary: One of the successor states to Alexander's empire, ruling over Syria and the eastern territories, including Judea. It was the oppressor during the Maccabean Revolt.

entities.title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
entities.summary: Another successor state, ruling Egypt and North Africa, often in conflict with the Seleucids over the Levant.

entities.title: Jethro
entities.summary: Moses' father-in-law, who advised Moses to delegate authority to capable men to help judge the people.

entities.title: Phineas
entities.summary: A priest who zealously defended the holiness of Israel by executing an Israelite man and a Midianite woman, stopping a plague and receiving a covenant of peace.

entities.title: Divine Council
entities.summary: The heavenly assembly of God and His angels, where true prophets stand to receive God's word and counsel.

entities.title: Fr. Stephen De Young
entities.summary: One of the hosts of the Lord of Spirits podcast, an Orthodox priest and scholar, who reads and comments on ancient texts in this episode.

entities.title: Ptah
entities.summary: An Egyptian god associated with craftsmanship and creation, elevated in the Memphite Theology as the supreme creator god, heart and tongue of the gods.

entities.title: Horus
entities.summary: Egyptian god, son of Osiris and Isis, associated with kingship and the sky; in the Memphite Theology, he is the firstborn son of Geb and is given rule over Lower Egypt.

entities.title: Osiris
entities.summary: Egyptian god of the afterlife and resurrection, whose death and rebirth are central to Egyptian mythology; his story is incorporated into the Memphite Theology to unify the gods.

entities.title: Geb
entities.summary: Egyptian god of the earth, father of Osiris, Isis, Seth, and Horus; in the Memphite Theology, he acts as the judge who divides the lands between Horus and Seth.

entities.title: Pharaoh Shabaka
entities.summary: The Kushite pharaoh of Egypt who ordered the inscription of the Memphite Theology onto stone around 710 BC, preserving the ancient text.

entities.title: Memphis
entities.summary: Ancient Egyptian city that became the capital after the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt; central to the Memphite Theology as the seat of Ptah's cult.

entities.title: Babylonian Servant
entities.summary: A character in the Babylonian dialogue who agrees with his master's every whim, offering contradictory advice, ultimately revealing the absurdity of life.

entities.title: Atrahasis
entities.summary: The hero of the Akkadian Atrahasis Epic, a wise man who is warned by the god Ea/Enki to build a boat to survive the flood.

entities.title: Ziusudra
entities.summary: The hero of the Sumerian flood story, a priest-king of Shuruppak who survives the flood and is granted immortality.

entities.title: Ignatius Donnelly
entities.summary: A 19th-century American congressman who wrote 'Atlantis: The Antediluvian World', popularizing the idea that Atlantis was a real civilization and the source of all ancient cultures.

entities.title: Madame Blavatsky
entities.summary: Founder of Theosophy, who incorporated Atlantis into her esoteric cosmology, linking it to the Aryan race and psychic powers.

entities.title: Edgar Cayce
entities.summary: An American psychic known as the 'Sleeping Prophet', who claimed to have visions of Atlantis and predicted its rise in the 1960s.

entities.title: Bergelmir
entities.summary: A frost giant in Norse mythology who survives the flood of Ymir's blood and becomes the ancestor of all frost giants.

entities.title: Nebuchadnezzar II
entities.summary: Nebuchadnezzar II (c. 605–562 BC) was the greatest king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, known for his military conquests, building projects, and role in the Babylonian exile of the Jews. He is a central figure in the Bible, especially in Daniel.

entities.title: Nabopolassar
entities.summary: Nabopolassar (c. 626–605 BC) was the founder of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, leading a revolt against Assyria and establishing Babylonian independence. He was the father of Nebuchadnezzar II.

entities.title: Assyrian Empire
entities.summary: The Assyrian Empire was a major Mesopotamian power known for its brutality and cultural appropriation. It conquered the Northern Kingdom of Israel and posed a threat to Judah, but eventually fell to a coalition of Babylonians and Medes.

entities.title: Tiamat
entities.summary: Tiamat is the primordial chaos dragon in the Enuma Elish, representing the saltwater ocean. She is slain by Marduk, who uses her body to create the heavens and the earth.

entities.title: Zoroaster (Zarathustra)
entities.summary: The prophet and reformer who founded Zoroastrianism, rejecting the old Vedic-style religion and establishing the worship of Ahura Mazda.

entities.title: Ahura Mazda
entities.summary: The supreme god in Zoroastrianism, creator of the universe out of light, and the embodiment of justice and goodness.

entities.title: Persia
entities.summary: The region and empire centered on the Iranian Plateau, founded by Cyrus the Great, and later known for its administrative and cultural achievements.

entities.title: Mithras
entities.summary: A god in Indo-Persian religion, later central to Roman Mithraism, associated with covenants and the sun.

entities.title: Mithraea
entities.summary: Caves or artificial caves used for Mithraic worship, found across the Roman Empire.

entities.title: Demeter
entities.summary: Greek goddess of harvest and fertility, central to the Eleusinian Mysteries, which reenacted the abduction of her daughter Persephone.

entities.title: Persephone
entities.summary: Daughter of Demeter, abducted by Hades, her journey to the underworld and return symbolized death and rebirth in the Eleusinian Mysteries.

entities.title: Dionysus
entities.summary: Greek god of wine, fertility, and ecstasy, associated with the Dionysian Mysteries, which involved intoxication, frenzy, and ritual violence.

entities.title: Hadrian
entities.summary: Roman emperor who founded a mystery cult for his deceased lover Antinous, building temples and establishing the city of Antinoöpolis.

entities.title: Antinous
entities.summary: Teenage favorite of Emperor Hadrian, deified after his death, leading to a mystery cult and widespread veneration.

entities.title: Apuleius
entities.summary: Roman author of 'The Golden Ass', which provides detailed descriptions of mystery cult initiations, particularly those of Isis and Osiris.

entities.title: Charles Finney
entities.summary: 19th-century revivalist who believed conversion could be achieved through techniques, a precursor to modern evangelical practices.

entities.title: Aquila of Sinope
entities.summary: Second-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, who was excommunicated from Christianity for practicing astrology and later converted to Judaism.

entities.title: Ishtar
entities.summary: Mesopotamian goddess associated with the planet Venus. The episode notes the connection between Ishtar and Venus in the naming of planets.

entities.title: William Lane Craig
entities.summary: An evangelical philosopher and theologian whom the hosts criticize for his views on God's relationship to time, particularly his Molinism and belief that God exists within time.

entities.title: St. Basil the Great
entities.summary: Church Father who expressed the idea that humanity is commanded to become God, which is only possible through the incarnation.

entities.title: St. Nicholas
entities.summary: Saint known for appearing in multiple places at once, demonstrating the saints' participation in divine omnipresence.

entities.title: Neanderthals
entities.summary: An extinct group of archaic humans who interbred with Homo sapiens. They had burial practices, including deliberate graves with grave goods, and are considered human.

entities.title: Shanidar Cave
entities.summary: A Neanderthal burial site in northern Iraq with multiple skeletons, some with grave goods, indicating deliberate burial practices.

entities.title: La Chapelle-aux-Saints
entities.summary: A Neanderthal burial site in France notable for a deliberate grave cut into limestone, containing an elderly individual with grave goods.

entities.title: Kebara Cave
entities.summary: A Neanderthal burial site in Palestine where a skeleton was found with arms folded, but the skull was removed, possibly for ritual purposes.

entities.title: Qafzeh Cave
entities.summary: An early Homo sapiens burial site in Palestine with 15 burials, including grave goods like shells and ochre, dating to around 100,000 BC.

entities.title: Panga ya Saidi
entities.summary: An early Homo sapiens burial site in Kenya, dating to around 84,000 BC, notable for the burial of a toddler with a pillow and blanket.

entities.title: Sumeria
entities.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian civilization with distinct burial practices: commoners buried under floors, elites in brick vaults with human sacrifices and grave goods.

entities.title: Ancient Egypt
entities.summary: Civilization known for elaborate burial practices including mummification, pyramids, and extensive grave goods, reflecting a death cult and belief in afterlife.

entities.title: Ancient Rome
entities.summary: Roman burial practices initially included cremation and burial outside the city, with ancestor masks in processions, later shifting to inhumation under Christian influence.

entities.title: Tobit
entities.summary: A righteous man in the deuterocanonical book who risked his life to bury the dead, considered a model of burial as an act of love.

entities.title: Leviticus 4
entities.summary: The chapter detailing the procedures for sin offerings for different classes of people: the anointed priest, the whole congregation, a leader, and a common person. It specifies the animals to be offered and the rituals to be performed.

entities.title: Leviticus 16
entities.summary: The chapter describing the Day of Atonement ritual, including the two goats: one for Yahweh (sin offering) and one for Azazel (scapegoat). The scapegoat carries the sins into the wilderness.

entities.title: Numbers 8
entities.summary: The passage describing the consecration of the Levites, where the people lay hands on them as a wave offering, and the Levites lay hands on the bulls for sin and burnt offerings. This shows that laying hands does not always mean transferring sins.

entities.title: Numbers 15
entities.summary: The passage contrasting unintentional sins with high-handed sins. Unintentional sins can be atoned for, but high-handed sins result in being cut off from the people.

entities.title: Hebrews 10
entities.summary: The passage warning that if we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins. This is used to show that the New Testament also distinguishes between repentant and unrepentant sin.

entities.title: Psalm 51
entities.summary: David's psalm of repentance after his sin with Bathsheba. It emphasizes that God desires a broken spirit, but also that after repentance, sacrifices will be offered again.

entities.title: Isaiah 1
entities.summary: The prophet's condemnation of Israel's hypocritical worship, where God rejects their sacrifices because they are unrepentant. This shows that sacrifices are not effective without repentance.

entities.title: Amos 5
entities.summary: The prophet's call for justice and righteousness rather than empty worship. God hates their feasts and sacrifices because they are unrepentant.

entities.title: Jeremiah 7
entities.summary: The prophet's reminder that God did not command sacrifices at the Exodus but commanded obedience. Sacrifices are not a substitute for obedience.

entities.title: Malachi 1
entities.summary: The prophecy that God will be worshipped among the nations with incense and pure offerings, indicating that true worship follows repentance.

entities.title: 1 John 1
entities.summary: The verse 'If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness' is used to show that confession is a condition for forgiveness, contradicting the idea that all sins are automatically forgiven.

entities.title: Father Thomas Hopko
entities.summary: A well-known Orthodox priest and theologian, mentioned in the opening banter about old audio recordings.

entities.title: Father Jeremy Davis
entities.summary: Author of 'Welcoming Gifts', a book exploring the true meaning of sacrifice, recommended by the hosts.

entities.title: Tertullian
entities.summary: Early Latin theologian who coined the term 'Trinitas' and later became a Montanist.

entities.title: Karl Rahner
entities.summary: 20th-century Jesuit theologian whose transcendental Thomism influenced Vatican II, often seen as a Hegelianizing of Catholic theology.

entities.title: Alexander Kalomiros
entities.summary: Author of 'The River of Fire', a widely circulated article that presents hell as the experience of God's love by the unrepentant. The hosts critique this view for depicting God as passive and distorting scriptural language.

entities.title: The Torah
entities.summary: The Law given through Moses, which functions on three levels: land, sin management, and imaging God. It is not a means of earning salvation but a way of life that facilitates theosis.

entities.title: The Church
entities.summary: The restored Israel, which continues the Torah in a fulfilled way through the sacraments and a way of life centered on love and repentance.

entities.title: Tatian
entities.summary: An early Christian writer who composed the Diatessaron, a harmony of the four Gospels, which the hosts mention as an early example of harmonization.

entities.title: St. Mark
entities.summary: The author of the earliest Gospel, traditionally based on the memoirs of St. Peter, written after Peter's martyrdom.

entities.title: Barabbas
entities.summary: A notorious prisoner released instead of Jesus, whose name means 'son of the father' and who represents the false messianic expectations of violent insurrection.

entities.title: St. Dysmas
entities.summary: The penitent thief crucified with Jesus, who is venerated as a saint and whose salvation is an exceptional case, not the norm.

entities.title: St. Longinus
entities.summary: The Roman soldier who pierced Christ's side with a spear, traditionally venerated as a saint.

entities.title: Secret Gospel of Mark
entities.summary: A modern forgery that claimed to contain additional passages from a secret version of Mark's Gospel, debunked as a fraud.

entities.title: Temple Curtain
entities.summary: The tearing of the temple curtain at Christ's death is interpreted as a sign of judgment against the temple and the high priesthood, not as opening access to all people.

entities.title: Acts of Paul
entities.summary: A second-century text containing traditions about St. Paul, including the Acts of Paul and Thecla, correspondence with Corinth, and the martyrdom of Paul. It is considered historically reliable in parts and was even read as canonical in some churches.

entities.title: Acts of Peter
entities.summary: A late second-century text collecting traditions about St. Peter in Rome, including his conflict with Simon Magus and his crucifixion upside down. It is anti-Gnostic and contains the famous 'Quo Vadis' episode.

entities.title: Acts of John
entities.summary: A mid-second-century text with traditions about St. John, including raising the dead and his peaceful death. It contains a later Gnostic insertion, which was used by the Manichaeans and was debated at the Seventh Ecumenical Council.

entities.title: Acts of Thomas
entities.summary: A text about St. Thomas's mission to India, including his being sold as a slave, building a palace in heaven, and performing exorcisms. It is ambiguous regarding Gnosticism and contains the Hymn of the Pearl.

entities.title: St. Thecla
entities.summary: A disciple of St. Paul, known for her virginity and preaching. She is a major figure in the Acts of Paul and is venerated as a proto-martyr, especially in the Antiochian Church.

entities.title: St. Nikephoros of Constantinople
entities.summary: A ninth-century Patriarch of Constantinople who compiled a list of apocryphal texts that are beneficial for private reading. His list is used as a guide for which apocrypha are acceptable.

entities.title: Ephraim
entities.summary: The tribe of Ephraim, descended from Joseph's son, became the largest and most powerful tribe in the northern kingdom of Israel. In prophetic literature, Ephraim often represents the entire northern kingdom.

entities.title: Mount Gerizim
entities.summary: The sacred mountain of the Samaritans, where they built their temple. It is located near Shechem and is central to Samaritan religious identity.

entities.title: St. Photini
entities.summary: The Samaritan woman at the well whom Jesus met in John 4. She is venerated as a saint in the Orthodox Church and is seen as a symbol of the conversion of the Samaritans.

entities.title: Hermas
entities.summary: The author of the Shepherd of Hermas, a freed Roman slave and brother of Pope Pius I. He received visions and recorded them in the text.

entities.title: Pope Pius I
entities.summary: Bishop of Rome in the mid-2nd century, brother of Hermas. His mention in the Muratorian Canon helps date the Shepherd of Hermas.

entities.title: Muratorian Canon
entities.summary: An early canon list from around AD 170 that includes the 27 books of the New Testament and comments on other texts, including the Shepherd of Hermas, which it says is not canonical.

entities.title: Father Bogdan
entities.summary: A contemporary Orthodox scholar whose work on the Shepherd of Hermas challenged the scholarly consensus regarding its Christology, arguing for a more orthodox reading.

entities.title: St. Athanasius
entities.summary: 4th-century bishop of Alexandria who recommended the Shepherd of Hermas for catechesis, showing its authoritative status despite not being canonical.

entities.title: St. Nicholas the Confessor
entities.summary: 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople who included the Shepherd of Hermas in his list of books to be read privately, showing its ongoing use.

entities.title: Codex Sinaiticus
entities.summary: A 4th-century manuscript of the Bible that includes the Shepherd of Hermas at the end, but this does not imply canonicity, as codices often included non-canonical texts for liturgical or devotional use.

entities.title: Antiochian Orthodox Archdiocese
entities.summary: The jurisdiction hosting the Parish Life Conference, known for its strong diaconate and convert-friendly culture.

entities.title: Metropolitan Philip
entities.summary: The late Metropolitan of the Antiochian Archdiocese who promoted the diaconate starting in the 1970s.

entities.title: Fr. David
entities.summary: A priest in Raleigh, North Carolina, referenced for his parish's large number of converts and confessions.

entities.title: Emperor Claudius
entities.summary: Roman emperor who expelled Jews from Rome, leading to the situation addressed in Romans.

entities.title: Galatians 5
entities.summary: A passage used to discern good online content by its fruits of the Spirit.

entities.title: John B. Calhoun
entities.summary: American ethologist who conducted the Universe 25 mouse experiments, studying the effects of overpopulation and social breakdown.

entities.title: Christopher Lasch
entities.summary: American historian and social critic, author of 'The Culture of Narcissism,' which analyzed the shift toward self-centeredness in American culture.

entities.title: Roman Reigns
entities.summary: Professional wrestler, quoted on the idea that people want you to do good but not better than them, illustrating the challenge of Christian love.

entities.title: Father Elias Batar
entities.summary: Orthodox priest, quoted on the proper attitude when reading the Epistle in church, emphasizing humility over performance.

entities.title: Orthodox Christian Deaf Association
entities.summary: Organization dedicated to ministering to deaf Orthodox Christians, mentioned in the Q&A about deaf ministry.

entities.title: Ancient Faith Radio
entities.summary: Listener-supported Orthodox media network that produces the Lord of Spirits podcast, mentioned at the end of the episode.

concepts.title: Materialism
concepts.summary: The belief that matter and energy are all that exists, leading to a worldview that excludes the spiritual. The hosts argue that modern Christians are often materialists by habit, living as if the physical world is all there is, which hinders their spiritual life.

concepts.title: Divine Council
concepts.summary: The heavenly assembly of spiritual beings (angels, 'gods') over which God presides. This concept is central to understanding the biblical use of 'gods' and the spiritual hierarchy.

concepts.title: Monolatry
concepts.summary: The worship of one God while acknowledging the existence of other spiritual beings that can be called 'gods'. The hosts argue this is a more accurate description of biblical faith than monotheism.

concepts.title: Spiritual Geography
concepts.summary: The idea that spiritual realities are tied to physical locations, such as mountains, springs, and caves, which serve as gateways or dwelling places for spiritual beings.

concepts.title: Sons of God
concepts.summary: A title for angelic beings who are members of the divine council, through whom God administers His kingdom. This language is taken from Canaanite culture (sons of El) and used in the Old Testament.

concepts.title: Ranks of Angels
concepts.summary: The nine traditional ranks of angelic beings (Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, Angels) are roles or jobs, not species. They are cosmic intelligences that serve God in various capacities.

concepts.title: Demons as Fallen Angels
concepts.summary: Demons are angelic beings who rebelled against God after creation, not before. They are not a different species but beings who failed to fulfill their created roles. There are multiple angelic falls, and God uses even their evil for good.

concepts.title: Succession Myth
concepts.summary: A common ancient Near Eastern narrative where a younger god overthrows the high god, often successfully. The Bible corrects this by showing that rebellion against the true God always fails.

concepts.title: Propaganda
concepts.summary: The idea that pagan myths are demonic propaganda, distorting true events to lead people into idolatry and rebellion against God.

concepts.title: Nephilim
concepts.summary: The offspring of the 'sons of God' and human women, described as giants. Their spirits become unclean demons after their death.

concepts.title: Unclean Spirits
concepts.summary: Demons that originate from the Nephilim, characterized by their uncleanness due to their illegitimate birth. They are the demons encountered in the Gospels.

concepts.title: Tower of Babel
concepts.summary: The biblical account of humanity's attempt to build a ziggurat to manipulate the divine, leading to the confusion of languages and the assignment of nations to angelic beings.

concepts.title: Satan's Fall in Christ's Ministry
concepts.summary: The event described in Luke 10:18 and Revelation 12 where Satan is cast down from heaven during Christ's ministry, marking a definitive defeat.

concepts.title: Theosis (Deification/Divinization)
concepts.summary: The Orthodox Christian understanding of salvation as becoming partakers of the divine nature, becoming like God, and being adopted as sons of God, which is the purpose of creation and humanity's destiny.

concepts.title: Promises to Abraham
