concepts.summary: The concept of how gods or God administer justice, contrasting Babylonian confusion with biblical revelation.

concepts.title: Platonic Dualism
concepts.summary: The philosophical view that the soul is the true self, trapped in a body, and that the body is a prison. This view has influenced Christian theology in problematic ways.

concepts.title: Resheph
concepts.summary: An ancient Near Eastern demonic deity associated with plague and pestilence, often depicted as an archer. In the Bible, Resheph is portrayed as a force under God's control.

concepts.title: Holy Unction
concepts.summary: The sacrament of anointing the sick with oil, as commanded in James 5:14-15. It is a means of healing for the whole person, connecting physical and spiritual restoration.

concepts.title: Holistic Healing
concepts.summary: Healing that addresses the whole person—body, soul, and spirit—recognizing that these aspects are interconnected and that true healing is restoration of the entire human being.

concepts.title: Kingship as Icon
concepts.summary: The concept that the king serves as an icon of God's rule, both representing God to the people and being venerated by them, but not worshipped as a god.

concepts.title: Symphonia
concepts.summary: The Byzantine concept of church and state working in harmony, with the emperor and patriarch having distinct but complementary ministries.

concepts.title: Coronation as Sacrament
concepts.summary: The anointing and crowning of a king or emperor is a sacramental act, conferring a ministry and office from God, similar to ordination.

concepts.title: Divine Right of Kings
concepts.summary: The idea that a king's authority comes directly from God, but this does not mean the king is above accountability; rather, it entails greater responsibility.

concepts.title: Separation of Church and State
concepts.summary: A modern concept that did not exist in the early church; the Byzantine model saw the emperor and patriarch as partners in governing a Christian society.

concepts.title: Nazarite Vow
concepts.summary: A vow in the Old Testament where a person separates themselves to the Lord, abstaining from wine and grapes, not cutting their hair, and avoiding contact with corpses. It is seen as a precursor to Christian monasticism.

concepts.title: Christian Monasticism
concepts.summary: The way of life of monks and nuns, characterized by asceticism, prayer, and separation from the world. It developed from the Nazarite tradition and was shaped by figures like St. Anthony the Great and St. John Cassian.

concepts.title: Asceticism
concepts.summary: The practice of giving up good things for better things, such as fasting, vigils, and almsgiving, to discipline the passions and grow closer to God. It is not about rejecting creation as evil but about preventing good things from becoming snares.

concepts.title: Samson as a Bad Monk
concepts.summary: Samson, a Nazarite from birth, is presented as a negative example who breaks all his vows, leading to his downfall. The hosts argue that he is not a saint and is seen by Church Fathers as a forerunner of the Antichrist.

concepts.title: St. John the Forerunner as Model
concepts.summary: St. John the Baptist is presented as the ideal Nazarite, keeping his vows and embodying the ascetic life. He is contrasted with Samson and serves as a model for Christian monasticism.

concepts.title: Hair and Sexuality in Ancient Culture
concepts.summary: In ancient Greek and Roman culture, long hair was associated with sexual availability and openness. St. Paul's instructions about hair in 1 Corinthians are understood in this context, addressing former pagans.

concepts.title: Acts 21 and Temple Sacrifices
concepts.summary: Acts 21 shows St. Paul participating in Jewish temple rituals, including Nazarite vows and sacrifices, after Christ's resurrection. This challenges the idea that all temple sacrifices were immediately replaced by the Eucharist.

concepts.title: Monastic Tonsure
concepts.summary: The ritual of cutting the hair during the monastic profession, symbolizing a new beginning and self-offering to God. It is the material act of the sacrament of monasticism.

concepts.title: Embodiment of Faith
concepts.summary: Christianity is not just a set of beliefs but a way of life and being. Monasticism exemplifies this by embodying the Christian life in a profound way, and all Christians are called to embody their faith.

concepts.title: Blood as Life and Purification
concepts.summary: Blood in the Old Testament is seen as the life of a creature, and its shedding in sacrifice brings purification and transformation out of death. It is used to consecrate objects and people, and its ambivalent nature (life from death) underlies the Torah's sacrificial system.

concepts.title: Water as Chaos and Life
concepts.summary: Water in Scripture has a dual symbolism: it represents primordial chaos and destruction (as in the flood), but also purification and life (as in ritual washings and springs in the desert). This ambivalence is resolved in Christ, who transforms chaos into life.

concepts.title: Great Blessing of Waters
concepts.summary: The Orthodox Christian service of the Great Blessing of Waters, typically performed at Theophany, sanctifies water by invoking Christ's baptism. The blessed water is used for purification and blessing of people, homes, and objects.

concepts.title: Christ Purifies Creation
concepts.summary: Christ's incarnation and baptism purify the material world, which had been subjected to the curse and the power of the evil one. By touching unclean things, He cleanses them, and His blood and water bring redemption and renewal.

concepts.title: Soul as Life
concepts.summary: The soul is not a separate immaterial substance but the life of a living being, as seen in Genesis 2:7 where Adam becomes a living soul.

concepts.title: Soul and Spirit Distinction
concepts.summary: Soul is the life of the body, while spirit is the organizing principle of a being or collective; they are not separate entities but aspects of the same reality.

concepts.title: Embodied Desiring
concepts.summary: The soul involves embodied desires and appetites, not just abstract life; this is rooted in the Hebrew and Greek terms for soul.

concepts.title: Eternal Life as Qualitative
concepts.summary: Eternal life is not endless duration but a quality of life defined by knowing God and Jesus Christ (John 17:3).

concepts.title: Soul as Connection to God
concepts.summary: The soul represents the connection of a living being to God, through which it receives physical and spiritual life.

concepts.title: Critique of Platonic Dualism
concepts.summary: Plato's view of the soul as a self-contained, immortal entity that uses the body as a vehicle is contrasted with the biblical view that the body is integral to identity.

concepts.title: Saints as Organizing Principles
concepts.summary: Through their connection to God in Christ, saints become organizing principles for larger collectives, similar to angels, as seen in heavenly patronage.

concepts.title: Antichrist
concepts.summary: The Antichrist is a figure who embodies opposition to Christ, often understood as a singular eschatological adversary but also as a type that appears throughout history. The term 'anti' means 'instead of,' indicating a usurper who seeks to replace Christ.

concepts.title: Man of Lawlessness
concepts.summary: A title from 2 Thessalonians 2, referring to the Antichrist as the ultimate embodiment of lawlessness (anomia), which means rejection of God's way of life (Torah). This figure is an archetype, not just an individual.

concepts.title: Apostasia (The Rebellion)
concepts.summary: The Greek word for 'rebellion' or 'apostasy,' used in 2 Thessalonians 2:3. It has military connotations of a defection or retreat from a post, which precedes the revelation of the man of lawlessness.

concepts.title: Katechon (The Restrainer)
concepts.summary: A term from 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7, often translated as 'restrainer' or 'impediment.' It has military connotations of a garrison or occupying force that holds back the mystery of lawlessness. The hosts interpret it as the liturgical worship of the Church, especially the Eucharist.

concepts.title: Negative Typology
concepts.summary: A concept where a person or event serves as an inverted type of Christ, highlighting Christ's character by contrast. The Antichrist is a negative type of Christ, and figures like Adam and Saul can serve as negative types in certain aspects.

concepts.title: Mystery of Lawlessness
concepts.summary: The hidden, active power of evil in the world, already at work according to 2 Thessalonians 2:7. It is the same as the 'spirit of antichrist' in 1 John, and it is held back by the katechon.

concepts.title: Age (Aeon)
concepts.summary: The concept of an 'age' in Scripture, often translated from the Greek 'aeon' or Hebrew 'yom' (day), refers to a distinct period characterized by a particular world order or state of things, not merely a measure of time.

concepts.title: New Covenant
concepts.summary: The covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel, characterized by the internalization of God's law and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, enabling believers to fulfill the righteous requirements of the Torah.

concepts.title: Chiliasm (Millenarianism)
concepts.summary: An early Christian belief that the Messianic Age would be a future, literal thousand-year earthly reign of Christ, often associated with material abundance. It was condemned by the Church as an eschatological error.

concepts.title: End of Days
concepts.summary: The concept of the end of days refers to the final period of history leading up to the last judgment. While the exact phrase does not appear in the Bible, it is derived from the creation narrative and the promise of a final day. The hosts discuss its origins in Second Temple Jewish literature and its use in Christian theology.

concepts.title: Justice as Order
concepts.summary: The biblical concept of justice (mishpat) is defined as the state of everything being in its proper place and functioning correctly. This understanding underlies the idea of judgment as the restoration of order in creation.

concepts.title: Macrocosmic Judgment
concepts.summary: The final judgment of the whole world, as depicted in the parable of the weeds, where the righteous and wicked are separated at the end of the age.

concepts.title: Microcosmic Judgment
concepts.summary: The ongoing judgment of individuals through correction and discipline, as illustrated by the pruning of vines. This type of judgment is aimed at repentance and growth in righteousness.

concepts.title: Judgment by Works
concepts.summary: The consistent biblical teaching that all people will be judged according to their deeds, both good and evil. This is not opposed to salvation by grace but is the basis for the final assessment of one's life.

concepts.title: Bodily Resurrection
concepts.summary: The belief that the dead will be raised in their physical bodies at the last day. This is essential for justice, as individuals must be resurrected to receive vindication or condemnation for their deeds.

concepts.title: Works Righteousness
concepts.summary: The idea that one can earn salvation through good deeds. The hosts clarify that while judgment is according to works, salvation is not earned; rather, the works are God's works performed through us.

concepts.title: Iconoclasm
concepts.summary: The rejection of icons and the principle that honor given to an image passes to the prototype. The hosts argue that this principle is foundational to Christian ethics and theology, and that iconoclasm undermines the doctrine of the Trinity and Christology.

concepts.title: Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse
concepts.summary: The four riders in Revelation 6, often identified as Conquest, War, Famine, and Death, but here identified as ancient Canaanite deities (Reshef, War, Raav, and Môt) filtered through Hebrew prophecy.

concepts.title: Canaanite Deities in Revelation
concepts.summary: The hosts argue that the Four Horsemen are based on Canaanite gods like Reshef, Môt, and Raav, but reinterpreted through the Hebrew Bible's prophetic lens.

concepts.title: Left Hand of God
concepts.summary: The concept that God uses even demonic forces to accomplish His will, allowing them to act within limits for purposes of judgment and repentance.

concepts.title: Gog and Magog
concepts.summary: Eschatological enemies of God's people, originating in Ezekiel 38-39 as a person (Gog) from a place (Magog), later developed in Jewish and Christian tradition as symbols of the final anti-God coalition.

concepts.title: Divine Judgment and Repentance
concepts.summary: The purpose of apocalyptic judgments is to call people to repentance, not to destroy them; God uses even evil to bring about good.

concepts.title: Invincibility in Christ
concepts.summary: The idea that by choosing to receive all circumstances as opportunities for growth and repentance, a Christian becomes invulnerable to harm, as nothing can separate them from God's love.

concepts.title: Parousia
concepts.summary: A Greek term used in the New Testament for Christ's coming, meaning 'being present in person' or 'arrival', emphasizing that Christ is not absent but will be present in a new way.

concepts.title: Epiphany (Epiphaneia)
concepts.summary: A Greek term meaning 'appearing' or 'manifestation', used in the New Testament to describe Christ's glorious appearing, drawing on Old Testament theophanies.

concepts.title: Apocalypse (Apokalypsis)
concepts.summary: A Greek term meaning 'revelation' or 'unveiling', used to describe Christ's revealing at the end of days, connecting to prophetic visions in the Old Testament.

concepts.title: Ascension
concepts.summary: The event where Christ was taken up into heaven, not as a departure but as His enthronement at the right hand of God, signifying His ongoing presence and rule.

concepts.title: Transfiguration
concepts.summary: The event where Christ revealed His divine glory to Peter, James, and John, serving as a glimpse of the resurrection and the world to come.

concepts.title: First Fruits
concepts.summary: An agricultural metaphor used by St. Paul to describe Christ's resurrection as the guarantee of the future resurrection of believers and the transformation of creation.

concepts.title: Spiritual Body
concepts.summary: The resurrected body that is permeated by the Holy Spirit, not a non-physical or ephemeral body, but a transformed physical body.

concepts.title: Hades vs. Hell
concepts.summary: The distinction between Hades, the intermediate state of the dead in this age, and hell, often conflated with eternal condemnation. The hosts clarify that Hades is not the same as the final state of the wicked.

concepts.title: Repentance
concepts.summary: Repentance is not merely feeling guilty or regretful, but actively repairing the damage caused by sin. It requires a body and is confined to this life, making it impossible for demons and the dead.

concepts.title: Eternal Condemnation
concepts.summary: The final state of those who reject God, described in Scripture with images like the lake of fire, outer darkness, and the second death. It is a real possibility and is contrasted with eternal life.

concepts.title: Universalism (Apokatastasis)
concepts.summary: The belief that all will inevitably be saved, which the hosts argue is a heresy condemned by the Church. They critique its philosophical presuppositions and pastoral consequences.

concepts.title: Lake of Fire
concepts.summary: A biblical image for eternal condemnation, often misunderstood as a literal place of fire. The hosts explain it as a metaphor for the experience of God's presence by the wicked.

concepts.title: Outer Darkness
concepts.summary: Another image for eternal condemnation, associated with weeping and gnashing of teeth, symbolizing madness and terror.

concepts.title: Second Death
concepts.summary: Eternal spiritual death, separation of the soul from God, as opposed to physical death. It is the fate of those who are condemned.

concepts.title: Localization of Deity
concepts.summary: Idols serve to localize a deity, bringing a spirit that is not physically present into a specific place, creating a version of that god tied to that location.

concepts.title: Limiting the Divine
concepts.summary: The idol acts as a visual definition, limiting the deity to specific qualities, which is necessary for humans to gain control or leverage over it.

concepts.title: Inversion of the Incarnation
concepts.summary: Idolatry is the reverse of the Incarnation: it attempts to reduce the divine to the human or subhuman, whereas the Incarnation elevates humanity to union with God.

concepts.title: Conceptual Idolatry
concepts.summary: Concepts can become idols when they are mentally shaped and delimited, allowing them to be manipulated. This applies to concepts like justice, love, or even God, when they are reduced to human definitions.

concepts.title: Idolatry and Sexual Immorality
concepts.summary: Throughout Scripture, idolatry is linked with sexual immorality, especially in the context of orgiastic pagan worship, which involves transgression of social boundaries to achieve ecstatic experiences.

concepts.title: Iconography vs. Idolatry
concepts.summary: The central distinction between iconography and idolatry: they are separate phenomena, not the same thing. Iconography involves images used for ritual participation and veneration, while idolatry involves worship directed to an image as a deity.

concepts.title: Myth and Ritual
concepts.summary: Myth is a story with ongoing significance for a community, kept alive through ritual. Iconography is a form of ritual reenactment, connecting viewers to the story and its spiritual reality.

concepts.title: Pagan Iconography
concepts.summary: The use of images in pagan religious contexts that are not objects of worship but serve as decoration or narrative, distinct from idols which are central to worship.

concepts.title: Israelite Iconography
concepts.summary: The use of images in the Old Testament, such as the cherubim on the Ark and the bronze serpent, commanded by God for specific purposes, showing that iconography is not inherently idolatrous.

concepts.title: Christian Iconography
concepts.summary: The continuation of Jewish iconographic traditions in Christian worship, grounded in the incarnation, and the development of icons as a means of participating in the heavenly reality.

concepts.title: Wonderworking Icons
concepts.summary: Icons through which God works miracles, such as healing or the flow of myrrh. These are not magical objects but means through which God acts, similar to the bronze serpent.

concepts.title: FOMO in Ancient Mesopotamia
concepts.summary: The concept of missing out on social events, or FOMO, is explored through ancient Mesopotamian texts that describe various reasons for being excluded from parties, such as unclean clothing, having an adopted monkey child, or telling offensive jokes.

concepts.title: Ancient Mesopotamian Humor
concepts.summary: The episode features a translation of an early first millennium BC stand-up comedy routine from Mesopotamia, showcasing the style and content of ancient jokes, which often involved self-deprecation and absurd comparisons.

concepts.title: Order and Chaos
concepts.summary: God's creation involves bringing order out of chaos, where chaos is non-being and order is the pattern of creation. This order is not external to God but is identified with His Wisdom/Logos.

concepts.title: Logos as the Pattern of Creation
concepts.summary: The divine Logos, identified with Christ, is the pattern through which God creates and sustains the universe. This is rooted in Proverbs 8 and developed in the New Testament.

concepts.title: Humanization of the World
concepts.summary: Humanity's purpose is to continue God's work of ordering and filling creation, thereby humanizing the world. This is tied to the concept of theosis and the image of God.

concepts.title: Meaning as Discovery and Creation
concepts.summary: Meaning is not purely discovered nor purely created, but arises from the active and passive engagement with the world and relationships. It is a communal, participatory process.

concepts.title: Application of Scripture
concepts.summary: The Church Fathers applied Scripture to their specific contexts, and this application is an instance of the pattern, not the pattern itself. Modern interpretation must similarly apply the text to contemporary life.

concepts.title: Technology as Instrumental Knowledge
concepts.summary: Technology is defined as the product of techne, encompassing not just physical tools but also ideas, concepts, and worldviews. It is instrumental knowledge that can be applied to objects, people, and spiritual beings, and it is not inherently good or bad but depends on how it is used.

concepts.title: Spiritual Technology
concepts.summary: In the ancient world, techne extended into the spiritual realm, including practices like magic, idolatry, and sacrifice. These were seen as instrumental means to manipulate spiritual beings or achieve results, contrasting with relational approaches like prayer and sacrifice that respect divine agency.

concepts.title: Instrumentalization of Persons
concepts.summary: Applying techne to human beings treats them as objects to be manipulated, leading to dehumanization and a mechanistic view of the cosmos. This is a key step toward materialism and determinism, where free will is denied.

concepts.title: Mechanistic Cosmos
concepts.summary: The instrumentalization of everything leads to a view of the universe as a deterministic machine, where all events are caused by prior events, leaving no room for free will or purpose. This is a hallmark of modern scientific materialism.

concepts.title: Collective Maturity
concepts.summary: The readiness for certain knowledge or technology depends on the collective maturity of humanity, not just individuals. This is illustrated by the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil and the idea that humanity was not ready for it, and by the need for spiritual wisdom to use technology well.

concepts.title: Freedom in Community
concepts.summary: True freedom is not individuality but the ability to serve God and flourish as humans, which can only happen in community. The Church is the primary place where this freedom can be realized, by rejecting enslaving ideologies and living together in love.

concepts.title: Spirit as Phenomenological
concepts.summary: Understanding 'spirit' not as a material or metaphysical entity but as a relational and experiential reality—how a being (angelic or human) relates to and influences a group, place, or person.

concepts.title: Koinonia (Participation)
concepts.summary: The Greek term for fellowship/participation, used to describe the synergistic relationship between humans and spiritual beings (God, angels, demons) through alignment of wills and activities.

concepts.title: Liberal Theology
concepts.summary: A post-Enlightenment theological approach that sees history as progressing toward a pinnacle (often the present culture) and interprets that development as the work of the Holy Spirit, leading to a rejection of tradition.

concepts.title: Baal Worship
concepts.summary: The worship of the Canaanite storm god Baal, which was a persistent temptation for Israel and was often intertwined with political and economic life. The episode discusses how Baal worship was practiced, its connection to the Phoenician trade empire, and how it was opposed by prophets like Elijah.

concepts.title: Theophany as Feast of the Incarnation
concepts.summary: The episode argues that Theophany, not Christmas, was originally celebrated as the primary feast of the Incarnation. This is based on early Christian evidence and the theological significance of Christ's baptism as the manifestation of God in the flesh.

concepts.title: Adam's Repentance
concepts.summary: The tradition that Adam repented after the fall, often depicted as standing in the Jordan River for 40 days. This is seen as a type of Christ's baptism and highlights the theme of repentance and restoration.

concepts.title: Christ's Victory over the Devil
concepts.summary: The episode presents Christ's baptism as a cosmic battle where Christ, as the new Adam, defeats the devil (identified with Baal) and wins the first victory for humanity. This victory is shared with believers through baptism and participation in Christ.

concepts.title: Incarnation and Identity
concepts.summary: The hosts discuss how the Incarnation affects our understanding of identity, both for Christ and for humans. Christ's identity is his entire existence, and through baptism, we put on Christ and find our true identity in him.

concepts.title: Euthyphro Dilemma
concepts.summary: A philosophical dilemma asking whether God commands what is good because it is good, or whether what is good is good because God commands it. The hosts argue both horns are problematic and propose a third way based on God's energies.

concepts.title: Divine Command Theory
concepts.summary: The view that morality is based on God's commands. The hosts critique it as making 'God is good' tautological and implying the universe is morally neutral apart from divine fiat.

concepts.title: Natural Law Tradition
concepts.summary: The idea that moral order is built into creation. The hosts acknowledge its biblical roots but argue it fails to account for the need for revelation and the unique revelation in Christ.

concepts.title: Consequentialism
concepts.summary: Ethical theory judging actions by their outcomes. The hosts critique it using the example of Joseph and the problem of God bringing good out of evil, making consequences unreliable.

concepts.title: Deontological Ethics
concepts.summary: Ethics based on duty and rules, associated with Kant. The hosts argue it fails in real-life situations like lying to save a life, and note that Christian tradition has always allowed exceptions for higher goods.

concepts.title: Jesus Embodies Israel
concepts.summary: Jesus recapitulates the history and experience of Israel, succeeding where Israel failed, and thus is recognized as the Messiah.

concepts.title: Jesus Embodies the Torah
concepts.summary: Jesus embodies the Torah as a way of life, teaching and living it perfectly, and fulfilling it by filling it full.

concepts.title: Jesus Embodies the God of Israel
concepts.summary: Jesus reveals the character of the God of Israel, particularly His humility, and embodies His relationship with His people.

concepts.title: Messiah as Identity
concepts.summary: The New Testament claim that Jesus is the Messiah is not about a checklist of fulfilled prophecies but about His identity, which is revealed through His embodiment of Israel, Torah, and God.

concepts.title: Fulfillment of Prophecy
concepts.summary: Prophecy is not a list of specific predictions but a pattern that Jesus embodies, and He fulfills all prophecies in a deeper sense.

concepts.title: The Number 40
concepts.summary: In Scripture, the number 40 (or 42) represents a period of preparation, anticipation, and repentance. It is often associated with fasting and purification, signaling that something significant is about to happen.

concepts.title: Baptism as Preparatory
concepts.summary: Baptism is not an end in itself but the beginning of a new life in Christ. It is a death to the old man (Adam) and a resurrection to new life, preparing the believer to receive the Holy Spirit and live according to the Spirit.

concepts.title: Pentecost as the Climax
concepts.summary: Pentecost, not Easter, is the true climax of the liturgical year. It is the feast of the giving of the Holy Spirit, which fulfills the promises of the New Covenant and represents the renewal of the covenant, making it the ultimate goal of Lent.

concepts.title: Self-Mastery
concepts.summary: The goal of the Christian life is self-mastery, which allows one to offer oneself fully to God. Lent is designed to reveal our weaknesses and help us develop self-control, which is the hardest fruit of the Spirit.

concepts.title: Torah as Foundation
concepts.summary: The Torah is the foundational text of all Scripture, with the rest of the Old Testament and the New Testament built upon it. The New Testament structures, including the Gospels and Epistles, are grounded in the Torah.

concepts.title: One Religion
concepts.summary: The religion of the Old Testament and the New Testament are the same religion. Christianity is not a new religion but the fulfillment of the faith of Israel.

concepts.title: Moral vs. Ceremonial Purity
concepts.summary: The Torah distinguishes between moral purity (related to sin) and ceremonial purity (related to ritual cleanliness). Both are necessary for approaching God, but they are not the same.

concepts.title: Sin as Disease
concepts.summary: Sin is portrayed in the Torah as a disease or a metaphysical taint that requires quarantine, purification, and healing. This understanding underlies the sacrificial system and the sacraments.

concepts.title: External to Internal
concepts.summary: The Torah's commandments, especially those about the tabernacle and sacrifices, were external structures that prepared humanity for the internal indwelling of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament.

concepts.title: Clean and Unclean
concepts.summary: The Torah's distinction between clean and unclean is not arbitrary but teaches discernment between moral and ceremonial purity. It is a practical way to cultivate a mindset of distinguishing between what is holy and what is not, which remains relevant for Christians.

concepts.title: Worship in the Torah
concepts.summary: Worship in the Torah is centered on dedicated places (tabernacle/temple) and specific practices, especially the offering of incense with prayers at morning and evening. This pattern continues in Orthodox Christian worship, particularly in Matins and Vespers.

concepts.title: Excommunication as Death
concepts.summary: The Torah's death penalty is interpreted as being 'cut off from among the people,' which is a spiritual death. In the New Testament, this is fulfilled in excommunication, which is meant to promote repentance and restore the sinner to the community.

concepts.title: Apocrypha Definition
concepts.summary: The term 'apocrypha' refers to books read privately, not heretical or forbidden texts. It is a middle category between public scripture and heretical works.

concepts.title: Testament Genre
concepts.summary: A testament is a genre of ancient Jewish literature presenting the last words of a biblical figure, often with prophetic elements, modeled after Jacob's blessings in Genesis 49.

concepts.title: Seven Parts of the Spirit
concepts.summary: The Testament of Reuben outlines seven parts of the human spirit: soul, sight, hearing, smell, taste, speech, and sex, emphasizing that these are good when properly directed.

concepts.title: Two Messiahs
concepts.summary: The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs present two messianic figures: a priestly Messiah from Levi and a kingly Messiah from Judah, with the priestly one elevated above the kingly.

concepts.title: Fullness of the Gentiles
concepts.summary: The Testament of Naphtali envisions the northern tribes being taken up into heaven, symbolizing that Gentiles will find salvation through Israel, a concept later used by St. Paul.

concepts.title: Book of Jubilees
concepts.summary: A Second Temple Jewish text that retells Genesis and early Exodus, adding traditions, interpretations, and an emphasis on the Enochic calendar. It is considered apocryphal but was widely used in both Jewish and Christian communities.

concepts.title: Enochic Calendar
concepts.summary: A 364-day solar calendar with four seasons of three months each, plus four intercalary days. It was considered mathematically perfect and was central to certain Jewish communities, including the Essenes at Qumran.

concepts.title: Apocalyptic Literature
concepts.summary: A genre that reveals heavenly realities and provides a 'heaven's eye view' of history, often through visions or journeys. The Book of Jubilees is apocalyptic in that it presents Moses receiving a vision of history from God.

concepts.title: Midrash
concepts.summary: A method of Jewish commentary that expands on Scripture with additional traditions and explanations, often incorporated directly into the text. Jubilees functions similarly as a commentary on Genesis.

concepts.title: Ritual Participation
concepts.summary: The idea that liturgical cycles and feasts allow believers to enter into eternal realities, not just commemorate past events. This is central to the Book of Jubilees and Orthodox theology.

concepts.title: Ascension vs. Assumption
concepts.summary: Distinction between being taken up to heaven while alive (ascension) and being taken up after death (assumption).

concepts.title: Assumption of Moses Tradition
concepts.summary: The tradition that Moses' body was taken up to heaven by God, referenced in Jude 9 and the Transfiguration.

concepts.title: Devil as Eater of the Dead
concepts.summary: The devil's claim to corrupt human bodies, based on Genesis 3:14, and the dispute over Moses' body.

concepts.title: Incorrupt Relics
concepts.summary: The phenomenon of saints' bodies not decaying as a sign of the bodily resurrection.

concepts.title: Orthodox vs. Roman Catholic Dormition
concepts.summary: Differences in understanding the Dormition of the Theotokos: Orthodox teaches she died and her body was assumed; Roman Catholic dogma allows ambiguity but leans toward no death.

concepts.title: Garments as Resurrection
concepts.summary: In the Ascension of Isaiah, garments symbolize the transformed, immortal body, not imputed righteousness.

concepts.title: Early Trinitarianism
concepts.summary: The Ascension of Isaiah contains early Christian Trinitarian thought, including worship of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

concepts.title: Pseudepigraphy as Interpretation
concepts.summary: Ancient texts attributed to figures like Isaiah or Moses are not fraudulent but use the figure as an interpretive device.

concepts.title: Exaltation of Humanity
concepts.summary: The destiny of the righteous is bodily resurrection and exaltation to be like the angels, not just going to heaven when you die.

concepts.title: Intellectual Humility
concepts.summary: The need to trust others and institutions, especially the Church, rather than relying solely on one's own understanding.

concepts.title: Devil Figure
concepts.summary: The concept of the devil as a fallen angel who rebelled out of envy against humanity and was cast down. This figure is identified with the serpent in Genesis 3 and is distinct from the Satan figure.

concepts.title: Satan Figure
concepts.summary: A title meaning 'adversary' or 'accuser,' referring to a spiritual being who tests and accuses humans, as seen in the book of Job. This figure is sometimes conflated with the devil but has distinct traditions.

concepts.title: Azazel Figure
concepts.summary: A demonic spirit associated with the wilderness and the Day of Atonement scapegoat ritual. In Second Temple literature, Azazel is depicted as a leader of fallen angels who corrupted humanity.

concepts.title: Mastema Figure
concepts.summary: A demonic figure in the Book of Jubilees, leader of the disembodied spirits of the giants. He is allowed by God to tempt and torment the wicked, serving as a tool of divine judgment.

concepts.title: Belial Figure
concepts.summary: A figure representing lawlessness and worthlessness, often depicted as the opponent of the Messiah in Second Temple literature. The name is used in the New Testament as a contrast to Christ.

concepts.title: Discernment of Spirits
concepts.summary: The practice of examining one's thoughts and actions to determine their spiritual origin, distinguishing between the Holy Spirit, one's own spirit, and demonic influences.

concepts.title: Magic as Technique
concepts.summary: Magic in the ancient world is understood as a set of techniques for manipulating spiritual beings, distinct from the role of a priest. It is accessible to anyone who learns the procedures, and it often involves ritual and material elements.

concepts.title: Divination
concepts.summary: Divination is the practice of gaining knowledge (past, present, or future) through spiritual means. It includes augury (reading omens), extispicy (reading entrails), and oracles, and was widespread in the ancient world.

concepts.title: Astrology
concepts.summary: Astrology in the ancient world was based on the belief that celestial bodies are divine or angelic beings that influence earthly events. Pagan astrology assumed fatalism, while Jewish astrology saw the stars as God's messengers.

concepts.title: Alchemy
concepts.summary: Alchemy is the production of objects or substances (like the philosopher's stone or potions) that are believed to manipulate spiritual forces. It is not primitive chemistry but a distinct magical practice.

concepts.title: Amulets
concepts.summary: Amulets were the most common magical objects in the ancient world, worn to ward off evil spirits or attract protection. They included pendants, rings, and talismans, often featuring images like the Medusa face.

concepts.title: Execration Bowls
concepts.summary: Execration bowls were clay bowls inscribed with curses and the name of a target, then smashed to symbolize the curse. They were a form of magical cursing in the ancient world.

concepts.title: Official vs. Unofficial Practitioners
concepts.summary: Magical practitioners could be official (attached to courts or institutions) or unofficial (itinerant or local folk practitioners). This distinction is based on social position, not licensing.

concepts.title: Prophecy vs. Divination
concepts.summary: In Deuteronomy 18, God forbids divination and instead promises a prophet like Moses. Prophecy is a direct relationship with God, while divination is manipulative and forbidden.

concepts.title: Magical Thinking in the Church
concepts.summary: The hosts warn against a mechanistic or formulaic understanding of sacraments and piety, which they label as 'magical thinking.' True Christian life is about repentance and relationship, not techniques.

concepts.title: Contentment as Anti-Magic
concepts.summary: Father Stephen concludes that contentment—being at peace with unmet desires—is the antidote to magical thinking, which seeks to control outcomes. Contentment is a superpower that frees us from the futile quest to fulfill every desire.

concepts.title: God and Time
concepts.summary: God is not bound by time; temporal categories do not apply to Him. God's actions manifest in time for created beings, but He Himself is outside of time.

concepts.title: Time as Phenomenological
concepts.summary: Time is not an objective thing but a human experience, similar to color or sound. It exists only in the realm of experience and varies among different creatures.

concepts.title: Apophatic Theology
concepts.summary: Apophatic theology emphasizes humility by recognizing that human language and concepts cannot fully encapsulate God. It involves making negative statements about God to avoid idolatry.

concepts.title: Theosis through the Calendar
concepts.summary: The liturgical calendar, with its cycles of feasts, structures human experience of time and facilitates theosis by uniting human life with divine life.

concepts.title: Human Experience of Time
concepts.summary: St. Augustine's phenomenology describes time as a tension between memory (past) and anticipation (future), with the present being a slippery point of attention.

concepts.title: Identity as External
concepts.summary: The hosts argue that a person's identity is not an inner, immaterial self but is constituted by their body, relationships, actions, and the web of connections in the world. This challenges modern individualism and Platonic notions of the soul as the true self.

concepts.title: Eternal Life as Transfigured Life
concepts.summary: Eternal life is not an endless succession of moments but the transformation of this present life, lived in time and space, into eternity. The good and sacred moments of life become eternal, while sin and suffering are burned away.

concepts.title: Purification After Death
concepts.summary: After death, the whole life is subjected to fire, burning away sin and suffering, while the good fruit remains. This purification is not a temporal process like purgatory but a way of thinking about how identity is purified and made eternal.

concepts.title: Religion as a Way of Being in the World
concepts.summary: A working definition of religion proposed by the hosts: a way of being in the world that encompasses all levels of reality and expresses itself in practices. This definition avoids reducing religion to beliefs or a separate sphere of life.

concepts.title: Axial Age
concepts.summary: A term coined by Karl Jaspers to describe the period from roughly 800 to 200 BC, when major religious and philosophical transformations occurred independently across the world, including in Greece, Israel, India, China, and Persia.

concepts.title: Comparative Religion
concepts.summary: The academic discipline of comparing different religions, which the hosts critique for often forcing superficial similarities and ignoring the unique contexts of each tradition.

concepts.title: Hunter-Gatherer Religion
concepts.summary: The religious practices of nomadic peoples before the Neolithic Revolution, characterized by a focus on a single sky deity or spirit, as opposed to the multiplicity of gods that emerged with settled life.

concepts.title: Continuity and Change
concepts.summary: The central theme of the episode: how the worship of the true God has remained continuous throughout history while undergoing legitimate changes, such as the transition from Second Temple Judaism to Christianity.

concepts.title: Second Temple Judaism
concepts.summary: The period of Jewish history from the rebuilding of the Temple to its destruction in 70 AD, characterized by diverse religious movements, including the emergence of Christianity as a form of Second Temple Judaism.

concepts.title: Primary and Secondary Scriptures
concepts.summary: The idea that within the canon, certain texts (like the Torah or the Gospels) hold a primary place, while others (like the Prophets or the Epistles) are secondary and interpret the primary texts.

concepts.title: Heresy vs. Other Religion
concepts.summary: The distinction between a heretical form of Christianity (like Arianism) and a completely different religion (like Gnosticism or Neoplatonism), based on continuity of scriptures, worship, and authority.

concepts.title: Modernism
concepts.summary: A cultural movement emphasizing the individual, egalitarianism, and theories of development, often seen as a rejection of Christianity.

concepts.title: Postmodernism
concepts.summary: A critique of modernism, often identified with post-structuralism, rejecting objectivity and universal truth, and emphasizing subjectivity and particularity.

concepts.title: Individualism
concepts.summary: The idea that the basic unit of humans is the individual, abstracted from all relationships, leading to egalitarianism and a focus on personal identity.

concepts.title: Egalitarianism
concepts.summary: The belief that all individuals are fundamentally equal and the same, leading to democracy and the idea that everyone's opinion is of equal value.

concepts.title: Theories of Development
concepts.summary: The idea that history progresses through stages and that we can understand and steer this development, often leading to chronological arrogance.

concepts.title: Structuralism
concepts.summary: A school of thought that attempts to salvage objectivity by locating meaning in language itself, rather than in the author's or reader's mind.

concepts.title: Post-structuralism
concepts.summary: A critique of structuralism, arguing that language cannot convey meaning objectively and that all signs are arbitrary, leading to a focus on subjectivity.

concepts.title: Tradition vs. Traditionalism
concepts.summary: Tradition is the living faith of the dead, formed in community, while traditionalism is the dead faith of the living, an individual's reconstruction.

concepts.title: Reactionary
concepts.summary: A response to modernism that often ends up assuming the very things it claims to hate, leading to a postmodern conservatism.

concepts.title: Daemon (Greek)
concepts.summary: In ancient Greek religion, a daemon was a spirit that occupied the realm between gods and humans. They were often the spirits of deceased heroes, who were venerated at shrines and could influence the living. The term later evolved to refer to guardian spirits or even gods themselves.

concepts.title: Genius (Roman)
concepts.summary: In Roman religion, a genius was a guardian spirit associated with a person, place, or people group. It was believed to share traits with its associated entity and could influence their fate. The genius of the emperor was a focus of imperial cult worship.

concepts.title: Guardian Demon
concepts.summary: The concept of a guardian demon was prevalent in Greek and Roman paganism, where each person was believed to have a spirit that guided and protected them. This was seen as a positive thing, unlike the Christian view of demons as evil.

concepts.title: Nephilim as Demons
concepts.summary: In Second Temple Jewish literature and early Christian thought, demons were identified as the disembodied spirits of the Nephilim, the offspring of fallen angels and human women. This view was held by many early Church Fathers.

concepts.title: Guardian Angel
concepts.summary: In Christian tradition, guardian angels are assigned to individuals to guide and protect them, replacing the pagan guardian demon. This is reflected in baptismal services and prayers to one's guardian angel.

concepts.title: Election as Adjective, Not Participle
concepts.summary: The hosts argue that the Hebrew and Greek words translated as 'chosen' or 'elect' are adjectives, not participles. This means they describe a quality or role of a person, not the result of an action done to them. This distinction undermines the Calvinist interpretation of election as God's arbitrary selection of individuals for salvation.

concepts.title: Israel Created, Not Picked
concepts.summary: The hosts argue that Israel was not chosen from among the nations but was created by God. Israel is not one of the 70 nations listed in Genesis 10; it is a new entity formed by God through Abraham and the Exodus. This challenges the idea that God arbitrarily picked one nation over others.

concepts.title: Elect Angels
concepts.summary: The phrase 'elect angels' in 1 Timothy 5:21 and Second Temple literature refers to angels who have a specific role or office, not to angels chosen for salvation. Since there is no salvation for angels, this usage demonstrates that 'elect' does not mean 'chosen for salvation' in the Calvinist sense.

concepts.title: Golden Chain of Redemption
concepts.summary: The 'golden chain' in Romans 8:29-30 (foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified) is often used by Calvinists to support predestination. The hosts argue that these verbs are all past tense and refer to God's past actions in salvation history, not to a logical order of decrees. They emphasize that the chain is about God's faithfulness, not individual selection.

concepts.title: Infra- and Supralapsarianism
concepts.summary: The hosts explain the Calvinist debates about the logical order of God's decrees regarding the fall and election. Infralapsarianism holds that God decreed the fall before election, while supralapsarianism holds that election was decreed before the fall. These distinctions are attempts to avoid making God the author of evil, but the hosts argue they are ultimately problematic.

concepts.title: Election as Qualification
concepts.summary: The hosts conclude that being 'chosen' or 'elect' means being qualified for a role or purpose. This is seen in military units, elders, and the Messiah. In the New Testament, Christians are called to make their election sure by growing in virtue and faithfulness, as Peter writes in 2 Peter 1.

concepts.title: Docetism
concepts.summary: An early Christian heresy teaching that Jesus only appeared to be human, denying his true physicality. The term comes from the Greek 'dokeo' meaning 'to seem'.

concepts.title: Adoptionism
concepts.summary: A heresy that Jesus was a mere man who was adopted as God's Son at some point, such as his baptism or resurrection.

concepts.title: Gnosticism
concepts.summary: A syncretistic religious movement in the second century that often viewed matter as evil and denied the incarnation. The hosts argue that Docetism should not be conflated with Gnosticism.

concepts.title: Theophany
concepts.summary: An appearance of God in the Old Testament, often with physical characteristics. The hosts discuss how these appearances relate to the incarnation of Christ.

concepts.title: Incarnation
concepts.summary: The doctrine that the Son of God took on human flesh. The episode explores the idea that Christ's humanity is not confined to his earthly life but is eternal and central to creation.

concepts.title: Second Yahweh
concepts.summary: A concept in Second Temple Judaism of a divine being distinct from God the Father, often identified with the Son of God. This figure appears in theophanies and is seen as pre-existent.

concepts.title: Lamb Slain from the Foundation of the World
concepts.summary: A phrase from Revelation 13:8 indicating that Christ's sacrifice is not merely a historical event but is rooted in the eternal purpose of creation.

concepts.title: Progressivism
concepts.summary: The belief that history is moving toward a better state, often seen as a secularized version of Christian eschatology. The hosts critique this view as a form of functional atheism that collapses God into history.

concepts.title: Presentism
concepts.summary: The anachronistic assumption that people in the past thought and experienced the world in the same way as people today. The hosts argue that this is a form of modernism, as seen in young earth creationism and other attempts to read modern science into ancient texts.

concepts.title: Functional Atheism
concepts.summary: Acting as if God is not involved in the world, even while believing in Him. The hosts argue that both progressivism and presentism can lead to this, as they imply that human effort alone can bring about change.

concepts.title: Moral Uncleanness
concepts.summary: Uncleanness resulting from sin, such as murder, sexual immorality, or idolatry, which makes one unfit to approach God and requires repentance and purification.

concepts.title: Ceremonial (Ritual) Uncleanness
concepts.summary: Uncleanness from unavoidable bodily functions, touching unclean things, or contact with death, which is not sinful but requires ritual washing before approaching God.

concepts.title: Holy vs. Common
concepts.summary: The distinction between things set apart for God (holy) and ordinary things (common), which is the proper framework for understanding clean and unclean, rather than good and evil.

concepts.title: Sin Offering
concepts.summary: A sacrifice offered upon reentry into the community after a period of uncleanness, which deals with sins committed during the separation, not the uncleanness itself.

concepts.title: Agos (Accursed)
concepts.summary: A Greek term for a state of permanent ritual impurity resulting from extreme moral crimes, such as murder, which bars one from sacred functions for life.

concepts.title: Churching of Mother and Child
concepts.summary: Orthodox practice of prayers for purification and reentry into the church after childbirth, rooted in Leviticus 12 and the presentation of Christ in the temple.

concepts.title: Demonic Activity Spectrum
concepts.summary: The spectrum of demonic influence ranges from temptation (thoughts) to torment (affliction) to possession (loss of agency) to participation (voluntary alignment with demons). This framework helps understand how demons interact with humans.

concepts.title: Thoughts vs. Ideas
concepts.summary: Thoughts are sense impressions that come into the mind unbidden, while ideas are formed by actively thinking about and connecting thoughts. This distinction is crucial for understanding spiritual warfare and the role of the nous.

concepts.title: Noetic World
concepts.summary: The noetic world is the spiritual realm perceived by the nous (mind), which is like a sensory organ. Demons primarily interact with humans through thoughts and the noetic realm, not physically.

concepts.title: Exorcism
concepts.summary: Exorcism in the Orthodox Church is a liturgical act that breaks the chains of sin and demonic influence. It is not magic or psychology but a means of dealing with sin and its consequences, applicable across the demonic activity spectrum.

concepts.title: Synergy with Demons
concepts.summary: Just as salvation involves synergy with God, one can synergize with demons by aligning one's will with demonic energies. This is the state of the Antichrist and the Nephilim, representing the extreme end of demonic participation.

concepts.title: Angelic Hierarchy
concepts.summary: The nine ranks of angels (Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, Angels) are not species but roles or jobs assigned by God, reflecting their participation in His glory and their tasks.

concepts.title: Angelic Agency
concepts.summary: Angels have their own free will and agency; they are not sock puppets or drones. Their obedience is voluntary alignment with God's will, just as human obedience is freely given.

concepts.title: Angelic Fall
concepts.summary: Angels fall by aligning their will with human wills in rebellion against God, often through idolatry and communion with demons. This happens in communion with humanity, and it explains how angels can be mutable.

concepts.title: Intercession of Angels and Saints
concepts.summary: Angels and glorified saints intercede for humans, bringing prayers before God. This is not in place of direct prayer to God but in addition to it, as an expression of love and communion.

concepts.title: Apocalypse of Abraham
concepts.summary: A Jewish apocalyptic text from the late first century AD, preserved in Slavonic by the Bogomils, depicting Abraham's rejection of idolatry, a cosmic Day of Atonement, and a vision of history.

concepts.title: Bogomilism
concepts.summary: A medieval dualist sect in the Balkans that preserved the Apocalypse of Abraham, holding Gnostic-like beliefs that the material world was created by the devil.

concepts.title: Cosmic Atonement
concepts.summary: The expectation of a final, all-encompassing purification of the cosmos, fulfilling the Day of Atonement, involving the defeat of evil and the restoration of creation.

concepts.title: Penal Substitutionary Atonement
concepts.summary: A Protestant doctrine, particularly Calvinist, that Christ took the punishment for the sins of the elect, requiring his spiritual death and separation from God, which Orthodoxy rejects.

concepts.title: Second Power in Heaven
concepts.summary: A Jewish theological concept of a visible divine being, distinct from God yet bearing His name, seen in figures like the angel Yehoel, later identified by Christians as Jesus.

concepts.title: Messiah ben Joseph
concepts.summary: A Jewish messianic figure associated with the northern tribes, who gathers Gentiles to worship God and suffers persecution, sometimes applied to Jesus by non-Christian Jews.

concepts.title: Crucifixion as Execution
concepts.summary: The historical practice of crucifixion as a method of execution, its origins with the Persians, and its use by the Romans as a deterrent and form of public humiliation.

concepts.title: Curse of the Torah
concepts.summary: The concept of the curse of the Torah, as enumerated in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28-30, which includes death and exile as consequences of disobedience, and how Christ bore this curse on the cross.

concepts.title: Participation vs. Substitution
concepts.summary: The distinction between substitutionary atonement (Christ dying instead of us) and participatory atonement (we die and rise with Christ), emphasizing the New Testament language of being 'in Christ'.

concepts.title: Manumission
concepts.summary: The act of releasing someone from slavery, used as a metaphor for Christ's redemption of humanity from slavery to sin and death.

concepts.title: Sequence of Signs
concepts.summary: In prophecy, a sign is an immediate event that confirms the certainty of a larger future fulfillment. Examples include the birth of Isaac and the virgin birth prophecy in Isaiah 7.

concepts.title: Non-Israelite Abrahamites
concepts.summary: Groups like Edomites, Moabites, and Ammonites are descendants of Abraham but not Israelites. They are distinct from Gentiles and initially worship Yahweh, receiving land and treatment similar to Israel.

concepts.title: Israel as a Nation
concepts.summary: Israel came into existence as a nation through the Passover and Exodus, constituted by shared experience and the giving of the Torah, which defined its way of life.

concepts.title: Torah as Nomos
concepts.summary: The Torah was given to Israel as its way of life (nomos), covering all aspects of society. It was unique to Israel and not given to other Abrahamite nations or Gentiles.

concepts.title: Messiness of History
concepts.summary: The hosts emphasize that history and theology are messy, not neatly systematic. Attempts to force them into systems lead to bad theology, such as dispensationalism.

concepts.title: The Torah is Keepable
concepts.summary: The hosts argue that the Torah was not given to show that humans cannot keep it, but rather as a guide for life in the land. They cite Deuteronomy 30:11 where God says the commandment is not too difficult, and point to biblical figures like David who kept the Torah perfectly through repentance.

concepts.title: Judgment on Giant Clans
concepts.summary: The conquest of Canaan is framed as a judgment against specific giant clans (e.g., Anakim, Rephaim) who practiced human sacrifice, cannibalism, and sexual immorality. The goal was to end these practices, not to commit genocide, as individuals could leave these groups and join Israel.

concepts.title: God's Giving vs. Human Receiving
concepts.summary: The hosts emphasize a distinction between God giving a gift and humans receiving it. This is illustrated in Joshua where God gave the land, but not all tribes took possession. This concept is crucial for understanding St. Paul's arguments about faith and works.

concepts.title: Land Promises Fulfilled
concepts.summary: The hosts argue that all land promises to Israel were fulfilled in Joshua's time, citing Joshua 21:43-45. This contradicts dispensationalist claims that some land promises remain unfulfilled, and it underscores the conditional nature of the covenant.

concepts.title: The Faithful Remnant
concepts.summary: Despite the collective disobedience of Israel and Judah, there was always a faithful remnant of individuals who kept the Torah. This concept is important for understanding St. Paul's collective language about the curse of the law.

concepts.title: Sabbath Years and the Exile
concepts.summary: The 70-year exile is explained as repayment for 70 missed Sabbath years, as Israel never observed the Sabbath year or Jubilee. This shows that God acts to establish the order prescribed by the Torah, even through judgment.

concepts.title: Hasmonean Dynasty
concepts.summary: A dynasty of Jewish priest-kings who ruled Judea from 140 BC to 37 BC, founded after the Maccabean Revolt. They combined the roles of king and high priest, which was controversial and led to opposition from the Pharisees.

concepts.title: Pharisees
concepts.summary: A Jewish sect known for their strict adherence to the Torah and oral traditions. They opposed the Hasmonean priest-kings and emphasized faithfulness to God's law, waiting for God's intervention. They are often misunderstood as legalistic hypocrites, but the hosts argue they were the 'good guys' in the New Testament context.

concepts.title: Sadducees
concepts.summary: A Jewish sect associated with the priestly aristocracy, descended from the Hasmonean line. They rejected the oral traditions of the Pharisees, did not believe in resurrection, and were often in conflict with the Pharisees.

concepts.title: Maccabean Revolt
concepts.summary: A Jewish rebellion against the Seleucid Empire and Antiochus IV Epiphanes, led by the Maccabees, which resulted in the rededication of the Temple and the establishment of the Hasmonean dynasty.

concepts.title: Restoration of Israel
concepts.summary: The prophetic expectation that God would restore the twelve tribes of Israel, including the northern kingdom, and establish a renewed covenant. St. Paul interprets this as fulfilled in Christ, with the inclusion of the Gentiles as the 'fullness of the nations'.

concepts.title: Olive Tree Metaphor
concepts.summary: St. Paul's analogy in Romans 11 of Israel as an olive tree, with natural branches (Jews) and wild branches (Gentiles) grafted in. It emphasizes the unity of Israel and the inclusion of the nations without replacing Israel.

concepts.title: Mosaic Authority
concepts.summary: The authority given by God to Moses to interpret and apply the Law, making binding rulings for Israel. It is not merely about performing miracles but about adjudicating how commandments apply in specific situations.

concepts.title: Prophetic Succession
concepts.summary: The transmission of prophetic authority from Moses to Joshua and then to subsequent prophets through the laying on of hands, establishing a chain of authority that continues in the Church.

concepts.title: Adjudication
concepts.summary: The act of making authoritative rulings on how God's commandments apply to specific situations, as exemplified by Moses and the prophets.

concepts.title: Laying on of Hands
concepts.summary: The physical act of transmitting authority from one person to another, as seen in the ordination of Joshua and later in the Church's ordination practices.

concepts.title: False Prophets
concepts.summary: Individuals who claim prophetic authority but lack the genuine spiritual experience and divine commission, often leading people astray with false assurances.

concepts.title: Apostolic Succession
concepts.summary: The chain of authority passed from the apostles to their successors (bishops) through the laying on of hands, ensuring continuity of teaching and authority.

concepts.title: Seat of Moses
concepts.summary: The authority of the Pharisees to make authoritative rulings, which Jesus affirms while condemning their hypocrisy.

concepts.title: Primacy and Conciliarity
concepts.summary: The balance between individual authority (primacy) and collective decision-making (conciliarity) in the Church, as seen in the apostles and bishops.

concepts.title: Prophetic and Priestly Authority
concepts.summary: The distinction and recombination of prophetic (representing God to people) and priestly (representing people to God) roles in the apostolic office.

concepts.title: Memphite Theology
concepts.summary: An ancient Egyptian theological text from the Old Kingdom, inscribed by Pharaoh Shabaka, that integrates various local deities and myths to establish Ptah as the supreme creator god, using theological argument to support the political unification of Egypt under Memphis.

concepts.title: Ancient Theological Method
concepts.summary: The way theology was done in the ancient world, particularly in Egypt and the Old Testament, by retelling familiar myths and stories with new emphases and polemical purposes to teach theological truths and support socio-political realities.

concepts.title: Babylonian Dialogue of Pessimism
concepts.summary: A darkly comedic Babylonian text featuring a master and servant debating the value of various actions, ultimately concluding that nothing matters, reflecting Mesopotamian pessimism and the absurdity of human striving.

concepts.title: Nihilism and Constant Affirmation
concepts.summary: Fr. Stephen's reflection on how surrounding oneself with 'yes men' and constant affirmation can lead to a nihilistic worldview, as illustrated by the Babylonian dialogue, and the importance of recognizing good and bad, right and wrong.

concepts.title: Ancient Flood Stories
concepts.summary: The episode surveys flood narratives from Sumerian, Akkadian, Babylonian, Greek, and Norse traditions, noting their common elements and contrasts with the biblical account.

concepts.title: Genesis Flood as Uncreation
concepts.summary: The hosts argue that the Genesis flood narrative describes God uncreating the world by reversing the separation of waters from days two and three, and then recreating it, rather than describing a merely global or local flood.

concepts.title: Documentary Hypothesis
concepts.summary: The hosts critique the JEDP documentary hypothesis, explaining its origins, circular reasoning, and why it is not useful for Orthodox Christian interpretation.

concepts.title: Atlantis and Occultism
concepts.summary: The episode traces the development of Atlantis from Plato's dialogues through its adoption by occultists like Madame Blavatsky and Edgar Cayce, and its connection to Nazi ideology.

concepts.title: Faith as Faithfulness
concepts.summary: Fr. Stephen De Young emphasizes that biblical faith is not mere mental assent but faithfulness demonstrated in one's life, and that debates over historical details are irrelevant to Christian living.

concepts.title: Babylonian Empire
concepts.summary: The Babylonian Empire, both the Old (c. 1894–1595 BC) and Neo-Babylonian (626–539 BC) periods, was a major Mesopotamian power. The Neo-Babylonian Empire, under Nebuchadnezzar II, conquered Judah and destroyed Jerusalem, leading to the Babylonian exile.

concepts.title: Marduk
concepts.summary: Marduk was the patron god of Babylon, originally a local agrarian deity who rose to prominence as the head of the Babylonian pantheon. He was associated with creation, wisdom, and kingship, and his myths, such as the Enuma Elish, were central to Babylonian religion.

concepts.title: Enuma Elish
concepts.summary: The Enuma Elish is the Babylonian creation epic, in which Marduk defeats the chaos dragon Tiamat and creates the world from her body. It was recited during the Akitu festival and served to legitimize Marduk's supremacy and Babylon's political dominance.

concepts.title: Akitu Festival
concepts.summary: The Akitu was a major Babylonian New Year festival, during which the Enuma Elish was recited and rituals reenacted Marduk's victory over chaos. It also included the 'Ordeal of Marduk' in Assyrian times, reflecting political subjugation.

concepts.title: Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel
concepts.summary: In the Book of Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar appears as a powerful but prideful king who dreams of a statue and a tree, both interpreted by Daniel as symbols of his empire and his temporary madness. His eventual repentance and acknowledgment of God's sovereignty are key themes.

concepts.title: Persian Empire
concepts.summary: The original Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great, was known for its vast territorial extent, administrative sophistication, and religious tolerance, contrasting with earlier empires.

concepts.title: Zoroastrianism
concepts.summary: A religion founded by Zoroaster, reforming earlier Iranian paganism. It emphasized the worship of Ahura Mazda, rejected animal sacrifices, and had practices like sky burials and the use of psychedelics.

concepts.title: Religious Tolerance
concepts.summary: Cyrus's policy of allowing conquered peoples to practice their own religions, which was unusual for ancient empires and contributed to the stability of his empire.

concepts.title: Messiah Concept
concepts.summary: The term 'messiah' (anointed one) is used in the Old Testament for various figures, including Cyrus, who is called 'the Lord's anointed' in Isaiah, showing that God can anoint even pagans for His purposes.

concepts.title: Mithraism
concepts.summary: A Roman mystery cult centered on the god Mithras, popular among soldiers, with rituals in underground caves, including a sacred meal and initiation grades.

concepts.title: Tauroctony
concepts.summary: The central image of Mithras slaying a bull, symbolizing cosmic creation and renewal, with astrological elements.

concepts.title: Mystery Cult
concepts.summary: A religious group with secret rituals and initiations, often involving personal salvation and esoteric knowledge.

concepts.title: Hypostasis
concepts.summary: In ancient paganism, a localized embodiment of a deity; used by modern scholars to describe how Mithras could be an aspect of the sun god.

concepts.title: Jesus Mythicism
concepts.summary: The fringe belief that Jesus never existed, often used to argue Christianity borrowed from pagan myths like Mithras.

concepts.title: Ritual and Perception
concepts.summary: Ritual, as repeated ordered activity, shapes how individuals perceive and interact with the world. It can be used deliberately to reshape perceptions, as seen in both Orthodox liturgy and mystery cults.

concepts.title: Near-Death Experience
concepts.summary: An experience of coming close to death and pulling back, which reframes one's perspective on life. Mystery cults aimed to induce this artificially through rituals, darkness, and substances.

concepts.title: Individual vs. Community
concepts.summary: Mystery cults were oriented toward individual experience and achievement, while Christianity is communal, emphasizing shared life and collective transformation.

concepts.title: Experience as Epiphenomenal
concepts.summary: In Christianity, spiritual experiences are not the goal but byproducts of participating in the sacramental life. They are not required for the validity of the ritual.

concepts.title: Evangelicalism as Mystery Cult
concepts.summary: American evangelicalism, with its focus on individual experience and techniques to induce altered states, parallels ancient mystery cults more than historic Christianity.

concepts.title: Omens
concepts.summary: Unusual occurrences or phenomena interpreted as signs of future events. In the context of astrology, omens in the sky were seen as messages from the gods, and their interpretation was a key step in the development of astrology.

concepts.title: Zodiac
concepts.summary: A circle of twelve 30° divisions of celestial longitude that are centered upon the ecliptic. The episode discusses its Babylonian origins and its adoption in Jewish and Christian contexts, including the association of the twelve tribes of Israel with zodiac constellations.

concepts.title: Fatalism
concepts.summary: The belief that all events are predetermined and therefore inevitable. The episode argues that astrology implies fatalism, which is incompatible with Christian belief in free will and human freedom.

concepts.title: Free Will
concepts.summary: The ability of humans to make choices that are not predetermined by external forces. The episode emphasizes that Christianity is an ethos of freedom, and that astrology's determinism is contrary to this.

concepts.title: Time and Space as Human Experience
concepts.summary: The hosts argue that time and space are not objective realities but categories of human experience, similar to color, which exists only in relation to a perceiver. They use this to explain why God, who is not finite, is not bound by these categories.

concepts.title: God's Eternity
concepts.summary: The concept that God's eternity is not endless time or Platonic stasis, but rather that temporal categories (past, present, future) do not apply to God. God does not exist at a point in time, and there is no future or past for Him.

concepts.title: Incarnation as Solution
concepts.summary: The incarnation is presented as the key to understanding how God can interact with humanity. By taking on human nature, the eternal Son of God enters into human experience, bridging the gap between the infinite and the finite.

concepts.title: Grave Goods
concepts.summary: Items placed in a grave intended for use in the afterlife, as opposed to mere personal possessions. The interpretation of grave goods in prehistoric burials is debated among scholars.

concepts.title: Prehistoric Burial Practices
concepts.summary: Burial customs of Neanderthals and early Homo sapiens, including body positioning, location, and grave goods, which show shared cultural rituals across vast geographic distances.

concepts.title: Kurgan Burial Mounds
concepts.summary: Burial mounds used by Indo-European peoples, typically for high-status individuals, often with internal chambers, altars, and grave goods, indicating ongoing ritual use.

concepts.title: Christian Burial Practices
concepts.summary: Orthodox Christian customs for burial, including vigil with Psalms, vesting clergy in vestments, burial facing east, and memorial services, all centered on the hope of resurrection.

concepts.title: Trans-temporality of Resurrection
concepts.summary: The concept that the effects of Christ's resurrection are not bound by linear time, so the righteous are already experiencing resurrection in a heavenly form, even before the general resurrection.

concepts.title: Burial Ministry
concepts.summary: A ministry within Orthodox parishes where members care for the dead, including preparing the body, conducting funerals, and burial, as an act of love and evangelism.

concepts.title: Scapegoat (Azazel)
concepts.summary: In Leviticus 16, the goat for Azazel had the sins of the people confessed over it and was sent into the wilderness, not sacrificed. This is the only place where sins are explicitly placed on an animal, and it is not a sin offering.

concepts.title: High-Handed Sin
concepts.summary: A deliberate, defiant sin committed with an uplifted hand, often associated with taking an oath. Such sins are contrasted with unintentional sins and are not covered by the sacrificial system because they indicate unrepentance.

concepts.title: Sacrifice as a Meal
concepts.summary: In the biblical context, sacrifice is not primarily about killing but about a meal of reconciliation. The killing of the animal is not the sacrifice; the priestly actions with the blood and fat constitute the sacrificial act, which is a gift to God and a shared meal.

concepts.title: Penal Substitution
concepts.summary: The theory that Christ took the punishment for sins in place of sinners, satisfying God's wrath. The hosts argue this is not biblical and leads to heresy, as it requires Christ to suffer spiritual death, which would separate Him from the Father.

concepts.title: Assurance of Salvation
concepts.summary: The confidence that one is saved, not based on a one-time decision but on a continuous life of repentance. True assurance comes from knowing God's love and His desire for all to be saved, not from a transactional guarantee.

concepts.title: Latin Theology
concepts.summary: The theological tradition that developed in the Latin-speaking West, characterized by the translation of Greek concepts into Latin and subsequent shifts in meaning.

concepts.title: Translation Slippage
concepts.summary: The phenomenon where the meaning of theological terms shifts over time as they are translated from one language to another, leading to a loss of original concepts.

concepts.title: Merit
concepts.summary: In Latin theology, the concept of merit as a quantifiable spiritual credit earned through good works or Christ's work, which became central to soteriology.

concepts.title: Nominalism
concepts.summary: A philosophical view that universals are mere names without corresponding reality, which influenced later Protestant theology.

concepts.title: Salvation as Theosis
concepts.summary: Salvation is not merely escaping hell but becoming like God through faithful participation in His life, a process called theosis. This is the original purpose for which humanity was created and remains the core of salvation throughout Scripture.

concepts.title: Faithfulness as the Key to Receiving Salvation
concepts.summary: Salvation is received through faithfulness to God's commandments and way of life, not through mere intellectual belief or legalistic works. This is demonstrated in the lives of Adam, Noah, Abraham, and Moses.

concepts.title: Three Levels of the Torah
concepts.summary: The Torah functions on three levels: the lowest concerns the land and life in it; the middle deals with managing sin through commandments and sacrifices; the highest and most important is about imaging God, summarized by justice, mercy, and faithfulness.

concepts.title: Christ as the Second Adam
concepts.summary: Christ succeeds where Adam failed, perfectly imaging God and fulfilling humanity's original purpose. The incarnation is the basis for theosis, and Christ's work removes the obstacles of sin, death, and demonic powers.

concepts.title: Saved From and Saved For
concepts.summary: Salvation involves being saved from sin, death, and demons, but also being saved for good works and participation in God's energies. The focus should be on the positive purpose of becoming like Christ and transforming the world.

concepts.title: Harmonization
concepts.summary: The practice of combining the four Gospel accounts into one unified narrative, which the hosts argue creates a non-canonical 'fifth gospel' and obscures the distinct theological points of each evangelist.

concepts.title: Eyewitness Testimony
concepts.summary: The concept that the Gospels are based on eyewitness testimony, which naturally varies in details and emphasis, and that this variation is a sign of authenticity rather than contradiction.

concepts.title: Modernism and Biblical Interpretation
concepts.summary: The hosts critique both liberal and fundamentalist approaches to Scripture as being modernist, focusing on proving historical facts rather than understanding the theological significance of the events.

concepts.title: Day of Atonement Typology
concepts.summary: The Passion narratives, especially Matthew's, present Christ as fulfilling both the scapegoat and the sacrificial goat of the Day of Atonement, with details like the scarlet robe and the reed pointing to this typology.

concepts.title: New Creation in John
concepts.summary: St. John's Passion account uses language from Genesis to present the crucifixion as the beginning of the new creation, with Mary as the new Eve and the blood and water from Christ's side as the birth of the Church.

concepts.title: Blood Crying Out
concepts.summary: The biblical theme that innocent blood shed unjustly cries out to God for justice and a reckoning, as seen with Abel's blood in Genesis 4.

concepts.title: Blood as Life
concepts.summary: The scriptural understanding that blood represents the life or soul of a creature, which is why it is forbidden to consume blood and why it is used in sacrificial atonement.

concepts.title: Avenger of Blood
concepts.summary: The person, often the nearest male relative, who is responsible for exacting justice for the shedding of innocent blood, and God as the ultimate avenger for those without human representation.

concepts.title: Sacrificial Blood
