The story of the Witch of Endor, where Saul consults a medium to summon Samuel, is discussed as an example of necromancy.
King Manasseh's sins include sorcery, divination, and necromancy, which he repented of.
Jesus is accused of casting out demons by Beelzebul, and he responds by pointing out the absurdity and warning against blasphemy of the Holy Spirit.
The story of Simon Magus, who practiced magic and tried to buy the Holy Spirit's power, is read and discussed.
The seven sons of Sceva attempt to exorcise using Jesus' name, are overpowered, and many new believers burn their magical books.
Paul lists sorcery among the works of the flesh, indicating its prevalence among former pagans.
The man of lawlessness will work signs and wonders through the energies of Satan, showing that miracles can be demonic.
The days of creation are not literal 24-hour periods but manifestations of God's work; the seventh day represents God's enthronement and kingdom.
The Greek word 'proorizo' means to put in order in advance, not to decree individuals to salvation or damnation; it refers to God providing the way of salvation.
The phrase 'unto the ages of ages' refers to the age to come, which has no end, not a finite period.
The 'so' in 'God so loved the world' is misunderstood; it means 'in this manner,' showing that love is an action, not a feeling.
Jesus says, 'If you love me, you will keep my commandments,' used to argue that love is expressed in actions.
Used to show that eternal life is a quality of the present life of the believer, not just a future hope.
Describes the purification of one's life by fire, where the work built on Christ is tested; used to explain the purification of the whole life.
The Old Testament saints were not made perfect until with us, connecting to the idea that Christ's resurrection is the beginning of the general resurrection.
The command for the Torah to be read publicly every seven years, which the hosts discuss as evidence that the Torah was not widely known in pre-exilic Israel.
Paul's address to the Athenians about the 'unknown god,' used as an analogy for how missionaries approached indigenous peoples with a memory of a high god.
Discussed as the beginning of calling upon the name of Yahweh, marking a shift in worship practices.
Paul's account of being in a trance in the temple, illustrating ecstatic visionary experiences.
Referenced in the discussion of the harrowing of Hades, where Christ preached to the spirits in prison.
The repentance of the Ninevites, used to illustrate that God honors repentance even from pagans.
The Archangel Raphael acts as a guardian angel, guiding and protecting Tobias, illustrating the guiding function of angels.
Peter uses the Greek term Tartarus to describe the place of imprisonment for the fallen angels, connecting to Greek mythology.
Jesus speaks of the angels of little ones who always behold the Father's face, a basis for guardian angels.
The table of nations lists 70 nations, and Israel is not among them, supporting the claim that Israel was created, not chosen from the nations.
God calls Israel 'my chosen,' but in context He is not happy with them, showing that 'chosen' refers to a role, not favoritism.
Paul refers to 'elect angels,' which cannot mean chosen for salvation, but rather angels with a specific role.
The 'golden chain' of redemption is interpreted as God's past actions in salvation history, not a logical order of decrees.
The quotation 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' is explained as referring to nations, not individuals.
Peter urges believers to make their calling and election sure through virtue, showing that election is conditional on faithfulness.
Jesus' post-resurrection appearance where he shows his hands and feet, emphasizing he has flesh and bones, not a spirit.
Peter's sermon: Christ's flesh did not see corruption, proving his bodily resurrection.
Paul speaks of Christ being 'from David according to the flesh', emphasizing his human lineage.
Christ is from the patriarchs according to the flesh, yet is God over all.
Christ broke down the dividing wall in his flesh, referring to the crucifixion.
Christ partook of flesh and blood to destroy the devil through death.
Christ suffered in the flesh, and we are called to share in that suffering.
Confessing Jesus Christ come in the flesh is the test of the Spirit of God.
Those who do not confess Jesus coming in the flesh are deceivers and antichrist.
Moses and elders see God, with a pavement under his feet, and they eat and drink.
The Lord comes and stands, calling Samuel, showing physical presence.
The Lord puts out his hand and touches Jeremiah's mouth.
The Lord appears to Abraham, eats, and has his feet washed.
The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, indicating the eternal nature of Christ's sacrifice.
God raised us up and seated us with Christ in heavenly places, already accomplished.
Quoted to support the idea that there is nothing new under the sun, countering the progressive view of history.
Referenced to illustrate that Christ's return will be like the days of Noah, an unexpected interruption.
Cited to emphasize the need for transformation by the renewing of the mind, which is central to the hosts' argument about change.
Used as an example of how St. Paul addressed specific issues in specific contexts, which must be recontextualized for today.
Used to establish the parallel between holy/common and clean/unclean, showing that clean/unclean is about set-apartness, not morality.
Quoted to show that approaching God while unclean is a sin, leading to being cut off from the people.
The basis for the 40-day purification period after childbirth and the churching of mothers.
Discussed in relation to bodily emissions and the parallel between male and female uncleanness.
Mentioned as the source for uncleanness from contact with the dead.
Cited for the uncleanness from defecation and the need to wash.
The story of Cain, the first mention of sin, and the curse that made him permanently unclean.
Describes Cain as 'the unrighteous one' and blames him for the flood, showing Second Temple interpretation.
Used to show that the clean/unclean distinction persists in the New Testament, with Christians called to separate from unclean things.
Compared to Wisdom 10 as a similar review of biblical history from a different perspective.
The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him. This is used to illustrate demonic torment as a form of tough love intended to drive repentance.
Sarah had been married to seven husbands, but the demon Asmodius killed each before consummation. This illustrates demonic affliction and ancestral sin.
Jesus' teaching about an unclean spirit returning with seven others if the house is left empty. This is applied to the need for positive replacement in spiritual life.
The seven sons of Sceva attempt to cast out demons using Jesus' name as a formula, but the demon attacks them. This shows that exorcism requires delegated authority, not magical incantation.
The coming of the lawless one is according to the working of Satan, with all power, signs, and lying wonders. This is used to illustrate synergy with demonic energies.
St. Paul urges intercessions for all, because there is one mediator, Christ; this is used to support the practice of intercession, not oppose it.
John the Baptist's declaration 'Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world' combines Passover and Day of Atonement imagery, fulfilled in Christ.
Discussed as the basis for the curse of hanging on a tree, applied to Christ's crucifixion.
Explained as God condemning sin in the flesh of Christ, not condemning Christ.
Interpreted as Christ canceling the record of debt, not paying a ransom to the devil.
Cited to show Christ's death destroys the devil and frees those enslaved by fear of death.
God's call to Abraham and the initial promises of descendants, land, and blessing.
God tells Israel not to harass the Moabites and Ammonites because He has given them land, showing they are Abrahamite nations.
The righteous will shine like stars in the resurrection, connecting to the promise to Abraham.
Used to argue that the Torah is not too difficult to keep, contradicting the idea that it was given to show human inability.
Lists the giant clans that Israel would displace, showing that the conquest was targeted at specific groups.
States that all land promises were fulfilled, used to refute dispensationalist claims of unfulfilled promises.
Describes the cutting off of the Anakim and the taking of the whole land, linking the conquest to the giant clans.
The Davidic covenant, promising an eternal throne, but with conditionality and discipline for sin.
Parallel to 2 Samuel 7, but emphasizes the son's eternal throne in God's house, pointing to the Messiah.
God tears the kingdom from Solomon and gives ten tribes to Jeroboam, but preserves one tribe for David's sake.
St. Paul speaks of the curse of the law, which the hosts interpret as the collective exile of Israel, not a metaphysical curse.
Prophecy of 70 years of Babylonian exile, used to explain the Sabbath year repayment.
Explains the 70 years as the land enjoying its Sabbaths, linking the exile to the neglected Sabbath years.
The vision of the dry bones, symbolizing the restoration of the whole house of Israel, including the northern kingdom.
The potter and clay metaphor, showing God's conditional plans for nations based on their repentance.
St. Paul's use of the potter metaphor, referencing Jeremiah, to explain God's purposes for Israel and the nations.
The olive tree metaphor, explaining the inclusion of the Gentiles and the future salvation of all Israel.
Jacob's blessing of Ephraim, saying his descendants will become the 'fullness of the nations', which St. Paul connects to the inclusion of the Gentiles.
God commands Moses to consecrate the firstborn, and Moses elaborates on how to apply this command, demonstrating his authority to interpret and apply God's word.
Jethro advises Moses to appoint capable men to help judge the people, showing the delegation of authority while Moses retains final authority.
God commands Moses to lay hands on Joshua and invest him with authority, establishing the pattern of prophetic succession.
Jeremiah condemns false prophets who speak visions of their own minds and give false assurances, contrasting with true prophets who stand in the divine council.
Jesus acknowledges the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat and instructs the crowds to obey their teachings.
Jesus gives Peter the keys of the kingdom and the authority to bind and loose.
Jesus gives the disciples authority to bind and loose in a conciliar context.
Jesus breathes on the apostles and gives them the Holy Spirit for the forgiveness of sins.
Paul reminds Timothy of the gift of God received through the laying on of hands.

Fr. Stephen references the Old Testament's use of ancient Near Eastern stories, such as the flood narrative, which are retold and inverted to teach theological truths, similar to the Memphite Theology's method.
The primary biblical passage discussed, the story of Noah and the flood, contrasted with ancient Near Eastern flood myths.
Jesus' reference to the days of Noah, interpreted as a warning about being unprepared for the second coming, not about Nephilim rituals.
The creation account that provides the framework for understanding the flood as an uncreation and recreation.
The Tower of Babel story is discussed as a spiritual account of the Bronze Age collapse, with the unfinished ziggurat in Babylon as a historical backdrop.
God calls Nebuchadnezzar 'my servant' and declares that He has given all lands into his hand, making him an instrument of judgment.
Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a statue, symbolizing a succession of world empires, culminating in the messianic kingdom.
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse to worship Nebuchadnezzar's idol and are thrown into a fiery furnace, where they are protected by a divine figure.
Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a great tree is interpreted by Daniel as a warning of his temporary madness, leading to his repentance and acknowledgment of God's sovereignty.
King Josiah is killed at the Battle of Megiddo against Pharaoh Neco, despite God's warning through Neco, illustrating the consequences of not trusting God.
This passage names Cyrus as God's shepherd and anointed, and declares that God will use him to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple, even though Cyrus does not know God.
Cyrus's decree allowing the Jews to return and rebuild the temple, fulfilling Jeremiah's prophecy.
The end of 2 Chronicles records Cyrus's proclamation, marking the end of the exile.
Mention of a Persian official named Mithridates, showing the name Mithra in the Bible.
Another mention of Mithridates, a court official, in the Greek text.
The story of Jephthah's daughter is presented as an alternate origin for the Eleusinian Mysteries, with the festival of torchbearers paralleling the search for Persephone.
Baptism is described as participation in Christ's death and resurrection, contrasting with mystery cult initiations.
The 'mystery' in the New Testament refers to God's plan revealed in Christ, not secret knowledge for an elite.
St. Paul's exhortation to think on what is true, noble, and pure is applied to the Christian calling to engage with the world.
The arrangement of the tribes in the wilderness camp mirrors the layout of the Babylonian zodiac, with four cardinal tribes and two on each side.
The call to lay aside every weight and sin that clings closely is used to illustrate the need to be free from the bondage of sin and demonic influences.
Used to support the idea of Christ's descent and ascent, and theosis, as the purpose of the incarnation.
Abraham buys the cave at Machpelah to bury Sarah, establishing a family burial site for the patriarchs.
After Jesus' resurrection, holy people left their tombs and entered the city, illustrating the trans-temporal effect of the resurrection.
Mention of a dispute over Moses' body, suggesting a special burial, which relates to his appearance at the Transfiguration.
Tobit's righteous acts include burying the dead, which is a model for Christian burial ministry.
Jesus' saying is interpreted not as forbidding burial, but as a rebuke to excuses for not following him.
Read in full to outline the sin offering procedures for different classes of people.
Discussed to show the scapegoat ritual and that sins are only placed on the goat for Azazel, not on the sin offering goat.
Used to demonstrate that laying hands on a sacrifice does not always mean transferring sins, as the Levites are offered as a wave offering without sins being pronounced.
Cited to show that theft is not punished by death, undermining the idea that all sins require death.
Contrasts unintentional sins with high-handed sins, showing that the latter are not covered by sacrifices.
Describes the high-handed sinner who blesses himself in his heart, showing the attitude of unrepentance.
Shows that God desires a broken spirit, but also that after repentance, sacrifices will be offered again.
God rejects the sacrifices of unrepentant Israel, showing that sacrifices are not effective without repentance.
God hates the feasts and sacrifices of the unrepentant, calling for justice and righteousness instead.
God emphasizes obedience over sacrifice, showing that sacrifices are not a substitute for following His ways.
Prophecy of pure offerings among the nations, indicating that true worship follows repentance.
Warns that deliberate sin after receiving the truth leaves no sacrifice, showing the New Testament also distinguishes between repentant and unrepentant sin.
Literal translation shows that everyone who sins practices lawlessness, not just those who 'keep on sinning'.
Confession is a condition for forgiveness, contradicting the idea that all sins are automatically forgiven.
Zacchaeus's repentance (giving half his goods and restoring fourfold) leads to Jesus declaring salvation.
Mentioned in a caller's question about the Greek word for 'serpent' (ophis) and a textual variant that reads 'drakon'.
Quoted at the end of the episode, describing the worship of the Lamb by angels and elders.
The command to fill the earth and subdue it is cited as one of Adam's positive commandments, indicating his purpose of theosis.
The negative commandment not to eat from the tree of knowledge is one of three commandments given to Adam, part of his way of life.
Abraham's faithfulness is credited as righteousness, a key text for understanding salvation by faithfulness.
The greatest commandments to love God and neighbor sum up the Torah and the Prophets, revealing the core of the law.
Christ condemns the Pharisees for neglecting the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
Gentiles who do not have the Torah can still fulfill its righteous requirements by nature, showing that salvation is not tied to the specific commandments.
Paul presents Christ as the second Adam, whose obedience brings life and righteousness to all, contrasting with Adam's disobedience.
We are saved by grace through faithfulness, not works, but created in Christ Jesus for good works, which are our purpose.
The elementary doctrines of repentance, faith, washings, laying on of hands, resurrection, and judgment are foundational but not the ultimate goal; we are to go on to maturity.
Jesus' cry from the cross is the opening verse of Psalm 22, which is a psalm of deliverance, not abandonment.
Matthew's citation of Jeremiah regarding the thirty pieces of silver points to the pattern of Israel devaluing God, yet God still blessing them.
John's citation of Zechariah identifies Jesus as the one pierced, who is God Himself, and points to the fountain of cleansing opened for repentance.
God prohibits eating blood because it is the life, and requires a reckoning for human blood shed.
The life of the flesh is in the blood, and God has given it for atonement on the altar.
David asks to be delivered from blood guilt, acknowledging his sin and seeking purification.
Jesus refers to all righteous blood shed from Abel to Zechariah, indicating the cumulative guilt of Israel.
The sprinkled blood of Christ speaks a better word than the blood of Abel, covering the cry for justice.
Christ's command to be witnesses in Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth is the geographic through-line of the Book of Acts, and the apocryphal acts show the fulfillment of this command.
St. Luke's reference to his first book (the Gospel) as covering what Christ began to do and teach is used to explain that Acts is the continuation of Christ's work through the Church.
The idea that not everything Jesus did is recorded is applied to the apostles, justifying the existence of traditions not in the New Testament.
Balaam's donkey speaking is referenced in the Acts of Thomas, where a talking donkey claims descent from Balaam's ass, showing the text's use of Old Testament imagery.
Describes the fall of the northern kingdom, the resettlement of foreigners in Samaria, and the origins of the Samaritans, including their syncretistic worship.
The Samaritans write to the Persian king to stop the rebuilding of Jerusalem, leading to a halt in construction and beginning the enmity between Jews and Samaritans.
Jesus' conversation with the Samaritan woman and his teaching about the harvest illustrate the gathering of the Samaritans into the kingdom.
Philip preaches in Samaria, and Peter and John come to lay hands on the new believers, showing the acceptance of Samaritans into the Church.
Mentions a Hermas in Rome, which some early writers like Origen thought was the author of the Shepherd of Hermas.
Agabus, a New Testament prophet, predicts a famine, showing that prophecy continued after the apostles, supporting the legitimacy of Hermas's visions.
Quoted by St. Peter at Pentecost, promising visions and dreams, indicating that such experiences are part of the new covenant era.
States that anyone hung on a tree is cursed, which St. Paul uses to explain Christ's crucifixion as taking on the curse of the law.
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, a key text in understanding the atonement.
Christians are strangers and exiles in this world, a theme echoed in the first parable of the Shepherd of Hermas.
Paul's teaching on Jews and Gentiles is applied to integrating newcomers and cradle Orthodox.
The fruit of the Spirit is used as a test for online Orthodox content.
The judgment scene is referenced to emphasize that we are judged by our actions, not just opinions.
Christ breathing on the disciples is connected to the breathing in baptismal exorcism.
Moses offers to be blotted out of God's book for the sake of the people, cited as an example of ultimate Christian love.
St. Paul wishes he could be cut off from Christ for the sake of his kinsmen, cited alongside Moses as a model of self-sacrificial love.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners, illustrating that real love gives without expecting anything in return.
The warning that a recent convert should not be made a bishop or teacher, applied to the advice against new converts creating online content.

glossary.definition: Hebrew word for 'God' or 'gods', used in the Old Testament to refer to the true God, angels, and even deceased humans.
Hebrew term meaning 'hosts' or 'armies', used in the title 'Lord of Hosts' (Yahweh Sabaoth), referring to God's command over the heavenly host.
The process of becoming like God through participation in His divine life, often connected to the idea of becoming 'gods' by grace.
The heavenly assembly of angelic beings (sons of God) over which Yahweh presides as the Most High.
A title for angelic beings who are members of the divine council, through whom God administers His kingdom.
A rank of angels associated with the throne of God, often depicted as fiery serpents (from Egyptian 'seraph').
A rank of angels who serve as throne guardians, often depicted as winged creatures (from Babylonian 'karubu').
A rank of angels associated with God's throne, often depicted as wheels with eyes, symbolizing God's omnipresence and omniscience.
A rank of angels in charge of judging and restraining other spiritual powers.
A rank of angels who preside over the material elements of creation (sun, moon, stars, winds).
Angelic beings assigned to preside over nations and peoples; they are the 'regional gods' of the ancient world.
A rank of angels, but the seven archangels (Michael, Gabriel, etc.) are not from this rank; they are higher and stand before the throne of God.
The lowest rank of angelic beings, whose primary role is to deliver messages from God.
Seven sages in Mesopotamian mythology who brought civilization and knowledge to humanity, often associated with the Watchers.
A Babylonian territorial spirit, mentioned in Deuteronomy 32:17 as the demons to whom the nations sacrificed.
A name for Satan in some Jewish traditions, meaning 'adversary of God', sometimes considered an archangel before his fall.
A name for Satan in Jewish tradition, meaning 'venom of God', often identified as the angel of death.
Greek term for adoption as sons, used in the New Testament and by Church Fathers in relation to theosis.
Greek term meaning 'God-making' or being made a god, synonymous with theosis.
Becoming holy; in Orthodoxy, understood as theosis, not just moral improvement.
In the ancient world, a neutral term for a spirit; later in Christian usage, it became negative, referring to fallen angels.
Greek word for resurrection, used in Psalm 82 to mean 'stand up' to judge, and applied to Christ's resurrection as the judgment of the gods.
The night before St. Nicholas Day, where Krampus, a demonic figure, is shown enslaved by St. Nicholas, symbolizing the defeat of pagan spirits.
The act of driving out demons, performed in baptism, house blessings, and other sacramental acts.
Honor given to saints and angels, distinct from worship which is reserved for God alone.
Death magic; attempting to communicate with the dead for forbidden knowledge or control.
The resurrection of the righteous to reign with Christ, as described in Revelation 20.
The Hebrew word for giants, often translated as 'fallen ones' but more accurately meaning 'giants' or 'tyrants.' In the Bible, they are the offspring of the sons of God and daughters of men.
A group of giant kings, often associated with the underworld. Og of Bashan is described as the last of the Rephaim.
Angelic beings in the Book of Enoch who rebelled and taught forbidden knowledge to humanity, leading to the birth of the Nephilim.
A Greek title for the Virgin Mary, meaning 'God-bearer' or 'Mother of God', affirming that she gave birth to Jesus Christ, who is fully God.
The mother of the king in the kingdom of Judah, who held a position of honor and authority, sitting at the king's right hand and acting as an intercessor.
In this context, a person or thing that serves as a visible representation of something else, particularly as a means of participation and continuation of the thing imaged.
The anointed one, a title for the expected king from the line of David who would deliver Israel and rule on God's behalf.
The apparent path of the sun across the sky over the course of a year, which is the basis for the zodiac.
A Hebrew word for constellations, used in Job 38:32, referring to the twelve signs of the zodiac.
A tradition that a prophet's death occurs on the same date as his conception, used to calculate the date of the Annunciation and thus Christmas.
A phrase used to describe the ancient understanding of a body as a collection of powers, energies, or abilities, rather than a physical object.
Having the form or likeness of God; humans are theomorphic, made in God's image.
Attributing human form or characteristics to God; the episode argues this is backwards, as humans are theomorphic.
Greek word for body, meaning the nexus of potentialities or collection of powers.
Greek word for flesh, a subcategory of body that is weakened, corruptible, and mortal.
The clothing God gave Adam and Eve after the Fall, representing a change to fleshly, mortal bodies.
Aristotle's concept of God as a perfect, unchanging being that moves others by being an object of desire, but is itself unmoved.
In Plato's philosophy, a lesser divine being who creates the world by looking at the Forms; later used in Gnosticism as a creator god.
A set of teachings attributed to Origen, often including the idea that God is bodiless and that resurrected bodies are spherical.
A group of monks who believed God has a body in a literal, physical sense, opposing the Origenist view.
A term used by St. Mark the Ascetic to describe the pre-incarnate Christ's body, meaning He had a body in the ancient sense.
The belief that humans are created in the image of God, and that biblical language about God's body parts refers to His powers, not physical features.
The ancient understanding of body as a center of powers and potentialities, not just a material object.
The state of being subject to death, given to humanity as a gift to enable repentance.
A demonic force that seeks to master humans, as depicted in Genesis 4, rather than merely a violation of rules.
Theological approach that emphasizes the limitations of human understanding and the mystery of God, leading to humility.
Latin for 'happy fault,' referring to the idea that Adam's fall led to the greater good of redemption in Christ.
The act of making someone propitious, i.e., pleased or well-disposed; in sacrifice, it refers to pleasing the deity.
The act of purification or atonement, often involving cleansing from sin or impurity.
Greek for 'table things,' referring to the side dishes and other foods served at sacrificial feasts.
Greek word for purification or cleansing, derived from the Semitic root QTR, meaning to offer incense.
A priest in ancient Rome who practiced divination by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals.
Bread placed on a table in the tabernacle/temple, replaced daily, eaten by priests, symbolizing God feeding his people.
A sacrifice offered to cleanse from the residue of sin, not a payment but a purification.
A sacrifice to restore relationship with God after a major rupture, often involving a communal meal.
A voluntary sacrifice offered in gratitude to God, often in fulfillment of a vow.
An offering of grain or flour, often associated with the harvest and first fruits.
An offering of wine or oil, often poured out on another sacrifice.
The feast commemorating Israel's liberation from Egypt, involving the sacrifice and eating of a lamb.
The feast fifty days after Passover, celebrating the giving of the covenant and later the Holy Spirit.
A harvest festival where Israelites lived in temporary booths to remember their dependence on God.
The holiest day of the Jewish year, involving fasting and atonement rituals, to be discussed in the next episode.
Hebrew root meaning 'to cover,' from which the word 'atonement' is derived. It refers to covering sin and purifying.
Greek word translated as 'atonement' or 'propitiation,' used in the New Testament to refer to the Day of Atonement and Christ's work.
A mistranslation of the Hebrew 'kapporet' (cover) in the King James Version, referring to the lid of the Ark of the Covenant.
Latin for 'out of nothing'; the doctrine that God created the world from nothing, meaning no pre-existing matter or being.
The study of purpose or design in natural phenomena; the idea that things have an end or goal that defines them.
Greek transliteration of the Hebrew 'Har Mo'ed', meaning 'Mountain of Assembly', the place where the final battle against God's enemies occurs.
A terraced pyramid-like structure in ancient Mesopotamia, representing a man-made mountain to reach the divine.
The Hebrew term for the underworld, the realm of the dead, often depicted as a dark, dusty place beneath the earth.
The Greek term for the underworld, also the name of its ruler. It is a place of shadows and forgetfulness, not necessarily a place of torment.
In Greek mythology, the deepest abyss of the underworld, used as a prison for the Titans. In the New Testament, it is the place where fallen angels are held.
The bottomless pit, the deepest part of the underworld, a prison for demons and rebellious spirits.
A place of comfort in the underworld for the righteous, where they rest with the patriarchs, often associated with a spring of water.
A lake in the underworld associated with purification and forgetfulness, later used in Christian apocalyptic literature as a place of cleansing.
The river in Greek mythology that separates the world of the living from the underworld, crossed by the ferryman Charon.
The river of forgetfulness in the underworld, which erases memories of past lives in reincarnation.
The river of wailing and lamentation in the underworld, one of the five rivers of Hades.
The river of fire in the underworld, which flows into the abyss and becomes the lake of fire.
Hebrew for 'Sea of Reeds', the body of water crossed by Israel, which also has a spiritual counterpart in Egyptian mythology as the sea of death.
A Canaanite god of pestilence, often translated as 'pestilence' in English Bibles, but recognized as a proper name in ancient context.
A Canaanite god of plague, often translated as 'plague' or 'destruction', but recognized as a proper name in ancient context.
Greek personification of death, used in the New Testament to refer to the power of death, often identified with the Canaanite god Moth.
The eleven resurrection gospel readings used in Orthodox Matins on Sundays, proclaiming Christ's victory.
A psalm verse chanted before the Gospel reading, often calling on God to arise, setting the theme for the reading.
Greek verb meaning 'to send', from which 'apostle' derives, indicating the commissioning of the apostles.
Arabic word for 'apostle' or 'messenger', used for both prophets and apostles, indicating direct reception from God.
A footprint or other shape carved into rock, often found at temple entrances, symbolizing a deity's path to enthronement.
The struggle of a god against a chaos monster, a common motif in ancient Near Eastern mythology.
A mythological pattern where a younger god overthrows the older high god to take the throne.
The concept that being in the presence of God without proper preparation is dangerous and can lead to death or destruction.
The visible manifestation of God's presence that filled the tabernacle and temple, and later descends upon believers at Pentecost.
A group of nomadic people in ancient Egypt, some of whom were associated with the worship of Yahweh.
Knowledge that can be demonstrated and proven, such as scientific or mathematical truths.
Opinion, perspective, or appearance-based knowledge, including testimony and viewpoint.
Craft, art, or know-how; the knowledge of how to make or do things.
Moral reasoning or practical wisdom; the ability to choose the good and shun evil.
Wisdom; the perception of the patterns and order in creation that lead to God.
The mind or spiritual perception; an organ that receives thoughts from the spiritual realm and can see God.
The principles or patterns in created things that reflect the Logos, Christ.
A serpent-like energy in Eastern practices that is said to rise up the spine to activate the third eye; a form of spiritual bootstrapping.
A concept in Eastern religions associated with the pineal gland and spiritual perception, often opened through techniques or drugs.
A Greek word meaning 'revelation' or 'unveiling'; a genre of literature that reveals spiritual reality.
The level of awareness before thoughts, allowing one to observe one's own mental processes.
The philosophical separation of mind and body, leading to a 'ghost in the machine' view of the soul.
In Kantian philosophy, the realm of things as they are in themselves, known through intuition, not senses.
In Kantian philosophy, the realm of things as they appear to the senses, the material world.
The part of the Divine Liturgy where the priest invokes the Holy Spirit to change the bread and wine.
The defeat of the giant clans, a spiritual reality behind the conquest of Canaan.
Pertaining to the intellect or mind; in Orthodox theology, refers to the spiritual faculty of the soul that allows direct knowledge of God and spiritual realities.
In Orthodox theology, the active operation or work of God in the world, distinct from His essence; often understood as grace.
A term coined by the hosts to describe the process of becoming like demons through sinful actions, the opposite of theosis.
The physical remains of a saint, such as bones or personal items, venerated because the body remains the person and is the Body of Christ.
A life lived in constant awareness of and participation with the angels, often associated with prophets and monastics.
The faithful minority preserved by God throughout history, as seen in Elijah's time and later in the New Testament.
A saint who serves as a guide and intercessor for an individual, modeled on the relationship between Elijah and John.
An ancient writing system using wedge-shaped marks, used in Mesopotamia, evolving from pictographs.
A Greek word meaning 'only begotten' or 'unique', used to describe Christ and Isaac, emphasizing their unique status.
A theory of atonement where Christ takes the punishment for sin in place of humanity, which the hosts argue is not the correct interpretation of the ram in the thicket.
In ancient pagan thought, a local manifestation or body of a god; in Christian theology, a person of the Trinity.
A phrase from Psalm 110 and Hebrews, referring to a priesthood that is eternal and not based on lineage, unlike the Levitical priesthood.
A year of remission of debts and release of captives, commanded in Leviticus 25, seen as a type of Christ's salvation.
The period from Christ's first coming to his second coming, during which he reigns as king and priest.
A sea serpent in Hebrew mythology, representing chaos and destruction. In the Bible, it is defeated by God and is a symbol of God's sovereignty over evil.
A land beast in Hebrew mythology, representing tyranny and chaos on earth. It is paired with Leviathan and is identified with the beast from the earth in Revelation.
The Canaanite god of the sea, often depicted as a dragon or sea monster. He is the embodiment of chaos and is defeated by Baal in Ugaritic mythology.
A system of assigning numerical value to letters, used in ancient Hebrew and Greek. It is used to encode names or words, such as the number 666 for Nero.
A mythical tree in Sumerian mythology, planted by Inanna, which becomes infested with creatures including Lilith.
A Sumerian demon name, the earliest form of Lilith, meaning 'maiden of the wind' or similar.
A collection of ecclesiastical law, including instructions for dealing with vrykolakas, issued to Orthodox priests in Greece.
A Greek term for a vampire-like creature, a demon-possessed corpse that returns to harm the living.
A pseudepigraphal text about King Solomon using a magic ring to command demons, which is not canonical but reflects certain motifs.
Greek word for 'messenger', from which 'angel' is derived.
Hebrew word for 'messenger' or 'angel'.
The four Hebrew consonants of God's name, YHWH.
Jewish writings from the period between 500 BC and 70 AD, including the Apocalypse of Abraham and Jubilees.
An appearance of God to a human being.
Hebrew phrase meaning 'word of the Lord'; refers to a divine person, the pre-incarnate Christ, who appears and speaks in the Old Testament.
Greek term for 'word'; in John's Gospel, it refers to the eternal Son of God, Jesus Christ, who is the agent of creation and revelation.
Aramaic term for 'word' used in the Targums to refer to the divine word, often inserted where God is described in human terms.
Aramaic paraphrase/expansion of the Hebrew Scriptures used in synagogues; often includes theological interpretations like the Memra.
A title used in the Old Testament and Second Temple Judaism, referring both to a mortal human and to a divine figure in Daniel 7. Jesus uses it as his primary self-designation.
A title for God the Father in Daniel 7, depicted as an elderly figure with white hair, sitting on a fiery throne.
A Second Temple Jewish belief that there are two divine figures in heaven, both identified as Yahweh. This concept underlies early Christology but was later rejected by rabbinic Judaism.
A Second Temple Jewish apocalyptic text, preserved by Orthodox Christians, that develops the Son of Man figure and is quoted in the New Testament.
A Greek word meaning 'authority' or 'freedom to act,' used in the context of 'second power in heaven' to denote a divine being with the same freedom as God.
Greek term meaning 'Lordly Man,' used by St. Mark the Ascetic to describe the pre-incarnate Christ in human form.
Hebrew for 'chariot,' referring to the throne-chariot vision of God in Ezekiel 1 and related mystical traditions.
Latin term for a sacred oath, used by Zwingli to emphasize the oath-taking aspect of the Eucharist.
Hebrew word for glory, meaning weight or mass, referring to God's bodily manifestation.
Hebrew term for the theophanic glory cloud, often translated as glory.
Christ's descent into the underworld to liberate the righteous dead and proclaim victory over demons.
Greek word for elder, used in the New Testament for church leaders; in English, it is the root of both 'priest' and 'presbyter'.
The arrangement of holiness in the Old Covenant: high priest, priests, Levites, Israel, and the nations, each serving as priests to the next outer circle.
Hebrew word meaning 'worthless' or 'vain,' used to describe false gods.
A Persian loan word meaning a walled garden; used in Scripture to refer to the Garden of Eden and the presence of God.
The portable tent shrine used by Israel for worship, patterned after the heavenly tent shown to Moses.
The innermost part of the tabernacle/temple where the Ark of the Covenant was kept, entered only by the high priest once a year.
The physical remains of saints, venerated because the saint's body has become a temple of the Holy Spirit and a testimony to the resurrection.
Greek word for liturgy; originally meant 'public works' in the city-state, later used for the service of the Levites and Christian worship.
Hebrew word for soul, meaning life. Used for both humans and animals.
Greek term for sorcery or witchcraft, often involving psychoactive drugs in magical practices.
Latin phrase meaning 'from the work worked'; a Western sacramental theology where the sacrament itself produces grace.
Greek term for energy or activity; in Orthodox theology, the divine energies are God Himself in action, distinct from His essence.
Greek title for the Theotokos meaning 'All-Holy'; signifies she is set apart for God's purpose.
Theory that there were other humans besides Adam and Eve; often leads to theological problems regarding death and Christ's redemption.
Giant griffin-like bird in Jewish tradition; the Hebrew version of the Mesopotamian Anzu.
German for 'science'; in 19th-century German academia, the idea that history should be a scientific discipline.
Greek for 'mindset' or 'way of thinking'; the patristic mindset for reading Scripture.
Latin for 'consensus of the Fathers'; the idea that the Fathers' collective interpretation gives the meaning of Scripture.
The Christian doctrine that Christ descended into Hades after his crucifixion to rescue the righteous dead.
Texts not included in the biblical canon but considered edifying for private reading.
A symbol of God's mercy and the Holy Spirit, promised to anoint believers in the last days.
Hebrew verb meaning 'to kneel,' used for blessing, indicating a change in posture or orientation.
Greek word for blessing, literally 'good word' or 'endorsement,' used in the Septuagint to translate barak.
Greek word meaning 'blessed' or 'blissful,' used in the Beatitudes, referring to the divine life of the gods.
Greek word for fellowship, communion, or participation, used to describe the web of relationships in blessing.
The name of the demonic being to whom the scapegoat was sent on the Day of Atonement, symbolizing the removal of sin.
A Hebrew word meaning 'destruction,' used in the Bible as a name for the realm of the dead or a destroying angel.
The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown through supernatural means, often involving techniques like astrology or reading omens.
Akkadian term for a prophet, derived from the verb 'mahu' meaning 'to go insane' or 'to enter a frenzy', reflecting the ecstatic nature of prophetic experience.
Hebrew term for prophet, derived from Akkadian 'nabu' meaning 'to call out', emphasizing the prophet as one who proclaims a message.
A term for prophet (ro'eh or chozeh) emphasizing the visionary aspect of receiving divine revelation.
A person through whom a deity speaks, often in a state of possession, as seen in Greek religion, such as the Oracle at Delphi.
Speaking in tongues, which St. Paul distinguishes from prophecy, describing it as a gift directed toward unbelievers, requiring interpretation.
The belief in a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth, often associated with the Book of Revelation and considered heretical in Orthodoxy.
The list of books considered authoritative scripture in a religious community; in Orthodoxy, it is descriptive of what is used, not prescriptive.
The concept of the Torah as the 'law of the house' or household management, rather than a legal code, which informs Paul's use of 'household of God'.
A myth is a story with a living ritual component; when the ritual drops out, it becomes mythology, a mere story.
A demon associated with child sacrifice in the Old Testament, often mistranslated as 'ruler' or 'king.'
A folk belief that a malevolent glare can cause harm, often countered with prayers or amulets.
A curse concept in Indian Orthodox tradition, similar to the evil eye.
Originally referred to the integration of the five senses into a coherent perception of reality.
The ancient Near Eastern view of the world as having three levels: heavens, earth, and underworld.
Strong emotions or desires that can lead to sin, including both blameless (e.g., hunger) and blameworthy (e.g., greed) passions.
The separation of the soul from God, which is the real death and leads to physical death.
Hebrew word for 'crouching' in Genesis 4:7, derived from an Akkadian term for a demon that crawls up from the ground.
Greek word for ritual impurity incurred by sacrilege and murder, often permanent.
Hebrew word for 'mark' in the Mark of Cain, meaning a pledge, witness, or oath.
A fourth-century heresy that held the Son was similar to the Father but not of the same essence, and was created in time.
A name that includes the name of a deity, such as Jezebel (Baal) or Ben-Hadad (Hadad).
Thor's hammer, a symbol of his power over thunder and lightning.
The Norse end of the world, where Thor fights the Midgard Serpent and both die.
The second movement of the will that emerges after the fall, characterized by indecision and the need to choose between alternatives.
A person who, without explicit Christian faith, seeks to worship the true God and is accepted by Him, as illustrated by Cornelius.
Florovsky's distinction: dogma is non-negotiable core beliefs, doctrine is the teaching of dogma, and theology is reflection and application.
A female practitioner of magic or divination, often serving as a counselor or healer; in this context, a magical champion.
A translation of the Sumerian word for soul or life force, which Sagburu removes from the sorcerer, killing him.
Hebrew word for spirit, meaning wind or breath.
Greek word for spirit, meaning breath, wind, or blow.
Latin word for spirit, meaning breath or wind.
English word for spirit, originally meaning spirit in general.
A substance supposedly exuded by spiritualist mediums as evidence of spirits, later debunked.
The directedness and propulsion that moves any being toward its telos, related to its nature.
Theological term for the operations or activities of a being, especially God's energies.
A person who appears mad or foolish to the world but is actually set apart by God to speak truth and call people to repentance.
A class of angelic beings mentioned in the Book of Daniel and Enoch, who serve as heavenly council members and messengers of judgment.
In ancient Roman religion, a guardian spirit that was believed to guide a person, especially the emperor, and was associated with exceptional ability.
A historical medical diagnosis, derived from the Greek word for womb, used to label women who did not conform to societal expectations.
The surgical removal of the foreskin, given as a sign of the covenant with Abraham. It symbolizes cutting off from the world and being set apart for God.
The sacrament of initiation into the Christian faith, involving water and the invocation of the Trinity. It symbolizes death to sin and resurrection to new life in Christ.
Boundary markers of Jewish identity, such as circumcision, dietary laws, and Sabbath observance, which St. Paul argues are not the basis of salvation.
A state of impurity contracted through normal life events (e.g., touching a dead body) that required ritual washing to approach God.
A state of impurity resulting from sinful acts, requiring repentance and washing.
Greek terms for the renunciation of Satan and the joining of Christ in the baptismal rite, signifying a change of allegiance.
From the Greek 'eucharistia,' meaning 'thanksgiving.' The sacrament of the body and blood of Christ.
The Greek word for Passover, used by Orthodox Christians to refer to Easter, the feast of Christ's resurrection.
The Jewish ritual meal held on the first night of Passover, which developed after the destruction of the Temple.
The Roman Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, with no trace of bread and wine remaining.
A view often associated with Lutheranism that the body and blood of Christ are present alongside the bread and wine.
A communal meal in the early Church that accompanied the Eucharist, open to all, while the Eucharist was restricted to the faithful.
The bread from heaven that God provided for Israel in the wilderness, a type of the Eucharist.
A specially prepared oil consecrated by bishops, used in chrismation, consecration of churches, and other sacraments.
The Law of God, the first five books of the Bible, which the Holy Spirit empowers Christians to keep.
A priestly garment, part of the high priest's vestments, with twelve stones representing the tribes of Israel.
Objects kept in the breastplate of the high priest, used for discerning God's will, though their exact nature is unknown.
A crown worn by the high priest with the name of Yahweh inscribed on a gold plate, symbolizing his role as representative of God.
A ritual in which an offering is waved before the Lord, often the priest's portion, symbolizing that it belongs to God and is given back.
A Greek term meaning 'deposit' or 'charge', used in the ordination service when the bishop gives the newly ordained priest the consecrated bread to guard.
Greek term for penance in Orthodox practice, meaning a treatment plan or guidance for spiritual growth, not punishment.
A formal declaration of excommunication, intended to call to repentance, not a final condemnation.
Greek word for repentance, meaning a change of mind or heart.
Hebrew phrase meaning 'helper corresponding to him', indicating a partner who complements and fits together with the man.
Payment made by the groom's family to the bride's family as restitution for taking her from her household, not a purchase of a commodity.
Payment made to the groom along with the bride, often in political marriages, as part of a package.
Gift from the groom to the bride, giving her control over property or money, especially if he dies.
In Orthodox theology, a sacrament; an initiation and participation in divine reality, not a puzzle to be solved.
An Akkadian poem from ancient Mesopotamia that explores the problem of suffering and divine justice.
A gap in a manuscript or text where content is missing.
Hebrew word for soul, meaning the life of a living being.
Greek word for soul, similar to nefesh, referring to the life of the body.
Ancient Near Eastern deity of plague, depicted as an archer; in the Bible, a force under God's control.
Another demonic force associated with pestilence, often paired with Resheph.
An ancient Near Eastern treaty form where a great king makes a covenant with a lesser king, including historical prologue, stipulations, blessings, and curses.
Latin title meaning 'commander' or 'conqueror,' which became the basis for the title 'emperor.'
The title of the Roman Emperor as the high priest of the Roman state religion, responsible for offering sacrifices.
The council of nobles and bishops in Anglo-Saxon England who elected the king.
The elevated platform in a church from which the gospel is read and where the emperor was anointed and crowned.
Greek word meaning 'worthy,' chanted during ordinations and the coronation of the emperor.
The Byzantine ideal of harmony between church and state, with the emperor and patriarch working together.
A person who took a vow to separate themselves to the Lord, abstaining from wine, not cutting hair, and avoiding corpses.
A way of life in which individuals dedicate themselves to God through asceticism, prayer, and community or solitude.
The cutting of hair during monastic profession, symbolizing dedication and new beginning.
The practice of self-discipline, such as fasting and vigils, to grow in virtue and closeness to God.
A title for St. John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Christ.
A service in the Orthodox Church that sanctifies water, typically performed at Theophany and in the baptismal service, invoking Christ's baptism to purify the waters.
A Lenten service where the Eucharist, consecrated on a previous Sunday, is distributed without a full Divine Liturgy, allowing communion on weekdays during Great Lent.
The annual Jewish ritual (Yom Kippur) for purifying the sanctuary and the people from sin, involving two goats and sacrificial blood.
The faculty of the mind (nous), considered a power of the soul in Greek thought, unique to humans.
Heresy that Christ lacked a human soul, which would undermine salvation.
The period between physical death and bodily resurrection, where the soul remains connected to God or separated.
Greek for 'lawlessness,' meaning rejection of God's way of life (Torah). It is the defining characteristic of the man of lawlessness.
Greek for 'presence' or 'appearing,' often translated as 'return' of Christ. It emphasizes Christ's manifestation rather than a mere coming back.
Greek for 'restrainer' or 'impediment,' with military connotations of a garrison. In this episode, it is interpreted as the liturgical worship of the Church.
A period of time characterized by a particular world order or state of things; often translated as 'age' in English.
A Protestant theological system that divides history into distinct dispensations or periods, often emphasizing a future earthly millennium and a separate plan for Israel.
A Latin term for 'age' or 'world order,' used by St. Augustine to describe the succession of worldly ages in contrast to the eternal city of God.
Hebrew word for justice, meaning the state of everything being in its proper place and functioning correctly.
A biblical term for a time of divine judgment, often translated as 'Day of the Lord'.
Literally 'God's works'; the idea that our good works are actually God's works performed through us.
An old English term for Judgment Day, derived from 'doom' meaning judgment or decree.
A Reformed doctrine that Christ was punished in our place to satisfy God's retributive justice.
Translation of Greek 'idou' and Hebrew 'hinneh', an interjection calling attention, often rendered as 'boom' in modern idiom.
Hebrew grammatical construction using the same verb twice for emphasis, e.g., 'dying you will die'.
A Roman silver coin, one day's wage for a laborer, used in Revelation 6:6 to show extreme food prices.
Hebrew idiom 'damim' referring to bloodshed as a spiritual agent of vengeance, not just literal blood.
Greek mythological spirits of vengeance, referenced in Psalm 87 (LXX) as belonging to God.
A 7th-century text that developed the story of Alexander the Great building a gate to imprison Gog and Magog.
A 7th-century apocalyptic text that elaborated the Alexander legend, placing the gate between two bronze mountains.
Greek term meaning 'appearing' or 'manifestation', used for Christ's glorious appearing.
Greek term meaning 'revelation' or 'unveiling', used for Christ's revealing at the end.
The common Greek dialect of the Hellenistic period, but the New Testament is written in a Semitic-influenced Greek.
Belief in a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth, often associated with end-times speculation.
The belief that all rational beings, including demons, will eventually be reconciled to God.
A term for eternal condemnation, derived from the Valley of Hinnom.
A phrase used by some to describe the traditional view of hell, often criticized by universalists.
The worship of idols, which in this context is understood as a technique of manipulating the divine realm through images and rituals, often involving attempts to control spiritual forces.
The use of sacred images in Christian worship, which is distinct from idolatry and will be discussed in the next episode.
Having the form of an animal, used to describe early idol depictions that combined human and animal features.
A form of pagan worship involving frenzied, transgressive rituals, often including sexual immorality and violence, believed to produce ecstatic spiritual experiences.
A term for wealth or material substance, personified as a false god in Scripture, representing the idolatrous pursuit of material security.
An image or object that is worshipped as a deity, often believed to embody a spirit, and is the focus of sacrificial offerings.
A story with ongoing significance for a community, kept alive through ritual and shaping the identity of the people.
Repeated communal behavior that enacts a myth, allowing participants to enter into the story and its spiritual reality.
The original person or event depicted in an icon; the honor given to the icon passes to the prototype.
A cake baked in honor of St. Phanourios, often offered as a thank-offering after finding a lost item, blessed and shared among the faithful.
Alternate spelling of cuneiform, used in the transcript.
A mode of interpretation that finds deeper spiritual meanings in a text, often applied to Scripture to make it relevant to new contexts.
Greek word for person, literally meaning 'face', emphasizing that personhood is relational and only fully known in community.
A term used in the Old Testament for angelic beings who surround God's throne; later applied to human saints.
A term from Second Temple Jewish literature for the 'Watchers,' a class of angels, sometimes used to refer to the spirits of nations.
German for 'spirit of the age,' used to describe the collective spirit or mood of a particular era.
A Semitic word meaning 'lord' or 'master,' used as a title for various deities, but specifically referring to the Canaanite storm god, son of El, who was worshiped in Phoenicia.
The doctrine that the Son of God took on human nature, becoming fully God and fully man, without ceasing to be God.
Hebrew word for 'good,' also meaning beautiful, whole, or intact, as used in Genesis.
Greek word for 'good' and 'beautiful,' used in the Septuagint.
Platonic dialogue named after a man prosecuting his father, often misused to pose the dilemma about God and morality.
Term derived from Nietzsche, implying moral neutrality and relativism; the hosts discourage its use in ethical discussions.
Greek word for power or ability, used by Aristotle to describe potentiality, related to the concept of energies.
Greek translation of Torah, meaning 'way of life' or 'custom', broader than law.
Jewish way of walking or living according to Torah, used by St. Paul in his epistles.
Christ's humanity as a protective veil, like the temple veil, revealing God's presence without causing death.
The Greek word for Passover, used by Orthodox Christians to refer to Easter, the celebration of Christ's resurrection.
The liturgical book used during the period of Great Lent, containing hymns and prayers for the season.
Instruction in the faith, originally a period of training in a way of living, not just intellectual learning, for those preparing for baptism.
The sacrament of anointing with holy oil, which in Orthodox Christianity is the reception of the Holy Spirit, typically immediately after baptism.
Purity from sin, which is required to approach God. Moral impurity is caused by sin and also makes one ceremonially impure.
Ritual cleanliness required to enter the tabernacle or temple. It can be lost through non-moral actions like touching a dead body, and is restored through purification rituals.
A sin committed with a 'high hand,' meaning unrepentant and defiant, which cannot be atoned for by sacrifices and results in being cut off.

glossary.term: Cut off from among the people
glossary.definition: A phrase in the Torah indicating exclusion from the community, which can mean exile or death, and is fulfilled in excommunication.
The act of excluding a person from the Church community, seen as a spiritual death intended to promote repentance and restoration.
Morning and evening prayer services in the Orthodox Church, which continue the Torah's pattern of offering incense with prayers at sunrise and sunset.
A genre of ancient Jewish literature presenting the last words of a biblical figure, often with prophetic and apocalyptic elements.
A name for the devil or a demonic figure in Second Temple Jewish literature, used in the Testaments to represent evil.
The liturgical language of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, in which the complete text of Jubilees is preserved.
A devil figure in Jubilees, leader of evil spirits, who makes a deal with God to afflict the wicked.
Commandments given to Noah and his descendants, considered binding on all humanity, as opposed to the Torah given to Israel.
Bodily ascent to heaven while still alive, as with Enoch and Elijah.
Taking up of a dead person's body into heaven, as with Moses and the Theotokos.
A genre of revelation, often involving a heavenly journey and unveiling of cosmic truths.
A manuscript page reused by scraping off the original text, often preserving earlier writings.
Works attributed to ancient figures, often used as interpretive devices rather than fraudulent claims.
Greek word for 'devil,' meaning 'one who throws apart' or 'slanderer.'
Hebrew word meaning 'adversary' or 'accuser,' used as a title for a spiritual being who opposes and tests humans.
A translation of Azazel, referring to the goat sent into the wilderness on the Day of Atonement, symbolically carrying the sins of the people.
Wonder-working; the ability to perform miracles, often attributed to saints. In the ancient world, it was seen as a form of magic.
Divination by observing the flight of birds and other omens.
Divination by reading the entrails of sacrificed animals, also called haruspicy.
A curse; in the ancient world, execration bowls were used to curse enemies by writing their name and smashing the bowl.
The sin of buying or selling spiritual offices or powers, named after Simon Magus.
A movement teaching that words and thoughts can manipulate reality, which the hosts identify as magical thinking.
A 19th-century movement emphasizing the power of mind over matter, which influenced prosperity gospel and New Age spirituality.
A theological approach that describes God by negation, emphasizing His incomprehensibility and transcendence.
Greek word meaning 'to put in order in advance,' often translated as 'predestined' in English, but without the fatalistic connotations.
Capable of being acted upon or experiencing emotions; a quality of creatures, not God.
A theological view that God does not know the future because it does not exist yet, which the hosts argue is incoherent and teaches a different God.
A colloquial term used by the hosts to describe the influence of Platonic dualism, which separates soul and body and sees the body as a prison.
The period in the mid-first millennium BC when various cultures developed philosophical and religious self-reflection, leading to new ideas about the body and soul.
The transition from nomadic hunting and gathering to settled agriculture and domestication of plants and animals, occurring around 10,000-8,000 BC.
The earliest period of the Stone Age, characterized by the use of chipped stone tools and a hunter-gatherer lifestyle.
The middle period of the Stone Age, transitional between the Paleolithic and Neolithic, with continued hunting and gathering but some development of tools.
The final period of the Stone Age, marked by the development of agriculture and permanent settlements.
The period of Jewish history from the rebuilding of the Temple to its destruction in 70 AD, marked by diverse religious movements.
A Roman Catholic concept referring to the condition of being free from mortal sin, which determines one's eternal destiny at death.
A person abstracted from all relationships, the basic unit of modernism.
The belief that all individuals are fundamentally equal and the same.
The idea that we can know things for certain using scientific methodology, and eventually know everything.
A school of thought that locates meaning in language itself, objectively.
A critique of structuralism, arguing that language cannot convey meaning objectively.
The dead faith of the living, an individual's reconstruction of tradition.
A theological term meaning that given the way the world actually is, a certain event was necessary, but it would not have been if the world were different.
Hebrew adjective meaning 'chosen' or 'elect,' used to describe someone given a role or office, not the recipient of an action.
Greek adjective meaning 'chosen' or 'elect,' derived from the verb 'eklegomai' (to call out), but used as an adjective to describe a person's quality or role.
The Calvinist view that God decreed the fall of man before decreeing election and reprobation.
The Calvinist view that God decreed election and reprobation before decreeing the fall of man.
The Calvinist doctrine that God has eternally decreed some people to damnation.
Greek verb meaning 'to seem' or 'to appear', root of the word Docetism.
Greek word meaning 'end' or 'purpose', used in philosophy to describe the final cause or goal of something.
A humorous phrase used by the hosts to describe a fully Hegelian view of history, where progress occurs through dialectical synthesis.
The anachronistic assumption that past people thought and experienced the world in the same way as people today.
Acting as if God is not involved in the world, even while professing belief in Him.
A Jewish ritual bath used for purification from ritual uncleanness.
The Orthodox prayer book containing services and prayers for various occasions, including churching.
Things indifferent, not morally good or evil; used in discussion of the Theotokos' birth without corruption.
The Western name for the Feast of the Presentation of the Lord, also called the Purification of the Virgin.
Greek term for a lesser spirit or ancestral spirit, which in Christian usage came to mean an evil spirit or demon.
A concept from occultism referring to a thought-form or collective entity created by group consciousness. The hosts question whether Tinkerbell could be an egregor, but it is not a Christian concept.
The world of thoughts and minds, where angels and demons operate, influencing human consciousness.
Greek for 'monk', meaning 'alone', but in practice, monks are not alone because they engage with the spiritual world.
An angelic being in the Apocalypse of Abraham, bearing the name of God, acting as a priest and guide.
A member of a medieval dualist sect in the Balkans that held Gnostic-like beliefs and preserved the Apocalypse of Abraham.
A Jewish messianic figure associated with the northern tribes, who gathers Gentiles and suffers persecution.
The act of releasing someone from slavery, used metaphorically for Christ's redemption.
The curses enumerated in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28-30 for disobedience, including death and exile.
A form of slavery in the ancient world where individuals sold themselves or family members to pay off debts.
In the Old Testament, the nations listed in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10), generally pagans, distinct from Israelites and other Abrahamites.
A giant clan mentioned in the Bible, descendants of the Nephilim, who were driven out by Joshua but some fled to Philistine cities.
A giant clan descended from Esau, uniquely belligerent toward Israel, and commanded by God to be destroyed.
Every seventh year, the land was to rest, and debts were to be forgiven. Israel never observed this, leading to the 70-year exile.
Greek term for Judaism, meaning the Judean way of life, encompassing all aspects of life according to the Torah.
The dispersion of the Jewish people outside of Judea, leading to the development of synagogues and a distinct Jewish identity.
The desecration of the Temple by Antiochus IV, who sacrificed a pig on the altar to Zeus, as mentioned in Daniel and the Gospels.
The Jewish festival commemorating the rededication of the Second Temple after the Maccabean Revolt, celebrated for eight days.
A ruler of a quarter of a territory, as used for Herod's sons after his death.
Hebrew term for ordination, originally referring to the authority imparted by the laying on of hands, from a root meaning 'sturdy' or 'able to support weight'.
Greek term for elders, used in the Septuagint for the leaders appointed to assist Moses, later used for church elders.
The Jewish practice of ordination through laying on of hands, which conveyed authority and grace.
Greek for 'overseer' or 'bishop', an office in the early church that succeeded the apostles.
The principle of decision-making by councils of bishops, as opposed to a single authority.
A geographical division of ancient Egypt, similar to a county or province.
A group of nine deities in Egyptian mythology, often worshipped together; in the Memphite Theology, the Ennead is said to have come into being through Ptah's creative word.
A theory that the Pentateuch was composed from multiple sources (J, E, D, P) over centuries, critiqued by the hosts as circular and unhelpful.
An esoteric movement founded by Madame Blavatsky, which incorporated Atlantis and the Aryan race into its teachings.
A German occult group that combined Atlantis and Hyperborea myths, influencing Nazi ideology.
An underwater rock formation near Bimini in the Bahamas, claimed by some to be evidence of Atlantis.
A Semitic people from Syria who migrated into Mesopotamia and founded the Old Babylonian Empire, including the dynasty of Hammurabi.
A Semitic language spoken in ancient Mesopotamia, used in the Old Babylonian and Assyrian empires, and the language of the Enuma Elish.
A language isolate spoken in ancient Sumer, the southern region of Mesopotamia, and the language of the earliest cuneiform texts.
A Babylonian New Year festival during which the Enuma Elish was recited and rituals reenacted Marduk's victory over chaos.
The Babylonian creation epic, in which Marduk defeats Tiamat and creates the world, establishing his supremacy.
The first Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great, named after the dynasty's founder Achaemenes.
In Zoroastrianism, the 'destructive spirit' or shadow of Ahura Mazda, not a separate co-equal deity.
The Zoroastrian concept of cosmic order and justice, similar to Ma'at in Egypt or Mishpat in Hebrew.
An ancient clay cylinder inscribed with Cyrus's proclamation after conquering Babylon, detailing his policies and legitimacy.
A plant used in Zoroastrian rituals to produce a hallucinogenic drink, cognate with Vedic soma.
Priests in ancient Persian religion, often associated with Zoroastrianism, who interpreted dreams and performed rituals.
A nomadic people of Central Asia who killed Cyrus the Great in battle.
A defensive wall built by the Neo-Babylonians to protect against invasions from the east, which Cyrus had to circumvent.
A Zoroastrian community that migrated from Iran to India, preserving their religion.
The second Persian Empire (3rd-7th century AD), known for its persecution of Christians and its conflicts with Rome.
A cave or artificial cave used for Mithraic worship, often underground.
The image of Mithras slaying a bull, central to Mithraic iconography.
A soft conical cap associated with Persia and later with liberty, worn by Mithras.
The 'mother rock' from which Mithras was born, worshiped in Mithraism.
Greek word for 'mystery', meaning a hidden thing that is later revealed, used in the New Testament for God's plan of salvation.
The ritual act of eating a live animal, practiced in the Dionysian Mysteries.
A spiced wine or drink given to initiates in the Eleusinian Mysteries, likely containing psychoactive substances.
The high priest in the Eleusinian Mysteries, an inherited office within a specific Athenian family.
A group of women permanently attached to the shrine at Eleusis, meaning 'all holy ones' or 'completely separated ones'.
A secondary effect that often accompanies a primary phenomenon but is not essential to it; used to describe spiritual experiences in Christianity.
Greek word meaning 'wanderer', from which the word 'planet' is derived, referring to the wandering stars that move differently from the fixed stars.
The self-emptying of Christ, referring to His humiliation and suffering, not to a cessation of His divinity.
A Calvinist doctrine that Christ's divine nature is everywhere while His human nature is confined to a specific place, which the hosts reject.
An early heresy that Christ only appeared to be human, not actually incarnate. The hosts argue that the physicality of Christ's resurrection body refutes this.
Crossing or transcending time; the idea that Christ's resurrection affects all times simultaneously.
Human experiences like hunger, thirst, and tiredness that are not sinful, which Christ assumed in his incarnation.
A burial mound used by Indo-European peoples, often for high-status individuals, with internal chambers and altars.
A hymn and prayer asking God to remember the departed, contrasting with pagan ideas of human memory keeping the dead alive.
Boiled wheat used in memorial services, symbolizing the resurrection.

The practice of reading one's own ideas into a text, rather than drawing meaning out of it. The hosts accuse many modern interpreters of eisegesis when they read substitutionary atonement into Leviticus.
Hebrew verb meaning 'to cover' or 'to atone', often translated as 'make atonement'. It involves purification and reconciliation, not payment of a penalty.
Greek preposition meaning 'in behalf of' or 'for the benefit of', used in the New Testament to describe Christ's death. It does not mean 'instead of'.
The separation of the soul from the body. Christ experienced physical death, but this does not mean we do not have to die.
Greek term for essence or substance, used in Trinitarian theology to denote the one essence of God.
Latin term for act or actuality, used in Latin theology to translate energeia, but with a different connotation.
Latin term for substance, used in Latin Trinitarian theology to denote the one substance of God.
Latin term for person, used in Latin Trinitarian theology to denote the three persons of the Godhead.
Greek term for worship, specifically the service due to God alone.
Greek term for veneration or service, often used for the honor given to saints.
Greek term for bowing or veneration, used in Orthodox theology for the honor given to icons and saints.
Latin phrase meaning 'faith alone', a key principle of the Protestant Reformation.
The Protestant doctrine that Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer and the believer's sin is credited to Christ.
A concept popularized by Alexander Kalomiros, suggesting that hell is the experience of God's love by the unrepentant. The hosts critique this as distorting Scripture.
The belief that all will eventually be saved, often associated with Origen. The hosts reject this as contrary to Scripture.
Introductory remarks or preliminary observations, often of a scholarly nature.
A harmony of the four Gospels compiled by Tatian in the second century.
A discredited theory that Jesus did not die on the cross but merely fainted and later revived.
The belief that biblical prophecies, especially those in the Olivet Discourse, were fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.
The state of being liable for the shedding of innocent blood, requiring a reckoning or atonement.
The act of covering or purifying sin through sacrificial blood, restoring the relationship between God and humanity.
Cities designated in the Torah where a manslayer could flee to receive a fair hearing and protection from the Avenger of Blood.
Relating to Gnosticism, a heretical belief system that the material world is evil and salvation comes through secret knowledge.
The movement against the veneration of icons, which was condemned at the Seventh Ecumenical Council. The Acts of John was used by iconoclasts in their arguments.
A major Gnostic religion founded by Mani, which used a version of the Acts of John with a Gnostic insertion.
The version of the Torah used by the Samaritans, written in the Samaritan script and containing about 6,000 differences from the Masoretic Text, including a tenth commandment about Mount Gerizim.
The Samaritan messianic figure, meaning 'restorer,' who is expected to come as a prophet like Moses, restore the kingdom of Israel, and bring about the resurrection.
A scholarly term for the books of Joshua, Judges, 1-2 Samuel, and 1-2 Kings, which are seen as a unified work interpreting Israel's history through the lens of Deuteronomy.
The Queen Mother in the kingdom of Judah, who held a position of power and was often mentioned in the biblical accounts of kings. This office is seen as a type of the Theotokos.
The belief that miraculous gifts and visions ceased with the death of the apostles or the close of the apostolic era.
The belief that miraculous gifts and visions continue throughout church history, as held by the Orthodox Church.
A guide of souls, often an angelic figure, who leads a person on a journey through the cosmos or the afterlife.
The Protestant doctrine that Scripture alone is the ultimate authority, which the episode argues is incompatible with the historical development of the canon.
A genre of literature that reveals hidden realities through visions and journeys, often involving a heavenly guide.
The renunciation of the devil in the baptismal service, literally meaning 'to be ordered away from'.
The alignment with Christ in baptism, literally meaning 'to be ordered with'.
A person receiving instruction in the faith before baptism.
The image of a serpent's mouth swallowing the damned in Last Judgment icons.
The early morning service of the Orthodox Church, also called Matins.
In Marxist theory, the process whereby human relationships are replaced by relationships with things, leading to isolation and loss of community.
A mouse utopia experiment by John B. Calhoun that collapsed due to overpopulation and social breakdown, used as a metaphor for societal decline.
Deaths resulting from suicide, drug overdose, or alcohol-related causes, often linked to social and economic despair.
A one-sided relationship where a viewer feels they know a media figure, but the figure does not know them, leading to distorted intimacy.
Terms used in Orthodox Christianity to distinguish those born into the faith (cradles) from those who converted later (converts).
